key problem. `scripts/upload_asset.py` refuses `Mesh` with that explanation.

**4. 1024 is the texture cap.** `SurfaceAppearance` maps are capped at 1024x1024
and larger source art is downscaled on upload. Bake at 1024. Baking at 2048 and
hoping costs bake time and buys nothing.

## Before the first run

| Variable | Needed by | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `HF_TOKEN` | stages 1 and 3 | Raises the ZeroGPU quota above the signed-out floor and buys queue priority. Effectively required. |
| `CF_ACCOUNT_ID`, `CF_API_TOKEN` | stage 1 only | Cloudflare Workers AI. Preferred for images because it costs **no** ZeroGPU quota, leaving all of it for the mesh. |
| `ROBLOX_API_KEY` | stage 5 | Open Cloud key with Assets write. |
| `ROBLOX_USER_ID` or `ROBLOX_GROUP_ID` | stage 5 | Who the asset is created under. |

`gradio_client` must be installed (`pip install gradio_client`). The Blender
commands below use `"$BLENDER"`: set the `BLENDER` environment variable to your
Blender 4.x executable (or put `blender` on PATH and use that). `batch.py` finds
Blender itself from `BLENDER`, then PATH, then the standard install folders.
Your value goes in `LOCAL.md`.

## Stage by stage

### 1-2. Concept image, then verify

```bash
python scripts/concept_image.py --prompt "a weathered brass steampunk revolver" --out work/concept.png
python scripts/concept_image.py --preset creature --prompt "a Holstein dairy cow" --out cow.png
```

Default backend is **FLUX.1-schnell on the official HuggingFace Space**, which
needs no credentials and is Apache-2.0, so its output is clean for a commercial
game. Two measured things decide this stage:

- **Pollinations' anonymous tier now serves only `sana`.** `/models` returns
  exactly `["sana"]`, and asking for `flux` silently gets the small model with no
  error. That is why an early batch of sixteen came back malformed. It is the
  fallback of last resort now, not the default.
- **Anonymous FLUX is queue-limited.** First request 12s, the very next one
  refused with "No GPU was available after 60s". The backend retries with
  backoff; `HF_TOKEN` (free account) buys priority, and
  `kaggle_run.py push --mode images` sidesteps the queue entirely by running
  schnell on your own Kaggle GPU.

The `--preset creature` framing is not cosmetic, and **a prettier picture can
make a worse mesh**. Hi3DGen reads an estimated *normal map*, not colour, so flat
vector-style art carries almost no shading to infer geometry from. The creature
preset asks for a shaded 3D toy render precisely to give the estimator gradients,
and pins the two failures that wasted a whole batch: all legs planted (the duck
and goose each generated standing on one leg) and no ground plane or scenery (the
pig generated on grass under a pink sky).

**Then read the PNG yourself and answer four questions:**

1. Is it the object that was asked for?
2. Is it **one** object, with nothing else in frame?
3. Is the **whole** object visible, uncropped?
4. Is the background plain and separable from the subject?

Any "no" means regenerate with a corrected prompt or a new seed. This costs
seconds. Do not proceed on a "close enough".

### 3. Image to 3D on Hi3DGen

Hosted, not local: Hi3DGen needs a 16GB NVIDIA GPU, and without one (for example a card with
less VRAM, or no CUDA) local generation is impossible rather than merely slow. Two venues,
and **the choice is about throughput, not quality** - the same weights either way:

**Kaggle (default for any batch).** 30 GPU-hours per **week** on a P100 or two T4s.

```bash
python scripts/kaggle_run.py push   --outdir work/farm --slug farm-animals
python scripts/kaggle_run.py status --slug farm-animals --wait 3600
python scripts/kaggle_run.py fetch  --outdir work/farm --slug farm-animals
```

Concepts go up as a private dataset, `kaggle_hi3dgen.py` goes up as a private
script kernel attached to it, and one GLB comes back per image. Needs a
**phone-verified** Kaggle account (that is what unlocks GPU and internet on
kernels) and `KAGGLE_API_TOKEN`, or the classic `~/.kaggle/kaggle.json`.

**A HuggingFace Space (one-offs only).** `python scripts/image_to_3d.py --image
work/concept.png --out work/high.glb`. Free ZeroGPU is **300 GPU-seconds per
day** against a generation of minutes, which is one or two meshes. Fine for a
single test, useless for a set of sixteen.

Expect a GLB of roughly 600k faces and tens of MB. Both paths also save the
normal-bridge image the model produced internally, which is the best diagnostic
when a mesh comes back wrong: if the bridge is wrong, the concept was the
problem and no reseed will fix it.

### 4. Blender: decimate, unwrap, bake

One command, runs headless, no live connection:

```bash
"$BLENDER" --background \
  --python scripts/mesh_pipeline.py -- \
  --input work/high.glb --outdir work/out --target-tris 9000 --texture-size 1024 \
  --decimate-mode collapse --target-studs 4.0
```

It writes `low.glb`, `normal.png` and `report.json` with the real triangle counts.

- **`--decimate-mode` matters.** `collapse` for organic shapes, `planar` for hard
  surface. On a gun or a crate, `collapse` rounds off exactly the edges that should
  stay crisp.
- **The UV unwrap is the weak link**, not the decimation, and the dial is
  `--uv-margin`. It is charged **per island** and a generated mesh has many, so a
  margin that looks small eats the texture. Measured on the test shape at 1024px:
  margin 0.02 used **29%** of the UV square, 0.003 used **49%**, 0.001 used 51%.
  Default is 0.003. Raise it only if islands visibly bleed into each other; lower
  it and you gain almost nothing. `report.json` carries `uv_coverage`, and under
  0.25 means the padding is the problem, not the decimation.
- **The cage matters.** Too small and the bake misses geometry (black patches), too
  large and it picks up the wrong surface (smeared detail). `--cage-extrusion`
  auto-scales from the model size; only override it if the bake is visibly wrong.

### 4b. Colour. Paint it, do not project it

Hi3DGen returns no colour, so colour has to come from somewhere. There are two
routes here and **the painter is the default**.

#### The painter (default)

```bash
# once per mesh: which way does it face in object space
"$BLENDER" --background \
  --python scripts/axes_probe.py -- --mesh work/out/low.glb --out axes.png

# read landmarks and the concept's real palette
"$BLENDER" --background \
  --python scripts/paint_texture.py -- --mesh work/out/low.glb \
  --concept work/concept.png --describe

# paint
"$BLENDER" --background \
  --python scripts/paint_texture.py -- --mesh work/out/low.glb \
  --spec work/pig.paint.json --outdir work/out
```

Every texel of the mesh's own UV layout is rasterised back to the 3D point it
belongs to, normalised into the bounding box, and coloured by a short stack of
stamps. **There is no camera anywhere in it**, so there is nothing to align,
nothing to smear, and no mirror-pair view to choose. Working example in
`references/example-pig.paint.json`.

- **`--describe` first, always.** It prints the bounding box, a ten-slice Y
  profile with the z and x extent of each slice, the nose-most vertex, the
  footprint of the lowest 5% of Z, and a six-colour k-means palette of the
  concept. That is enough to place a snout, eyes, ears and hooves without
  guessing, and it takes seconds.
- **`axes_probe.py` before that**, once per mesh. Three markers at known
  normalised positions, four views. It answers "which end is the head" from a
  picture rather than from a guess. On the pig: head at **y=0**, tail at y=1,
  z up, x across.
- **`mirror: "x"`** gives two eyes, two ears and two of anything from one entry.
- **`facing`** restricts a stamp to surfaces pointing a given way, which is how
  eyes stay on the sides of the head instead of wrapping around it.
- **The palette must come from `--describe`, not from looking at the concept.**
  A chroma test is not enough to drop the background: the pig concept's grey
  backdrop carries a pink cast off the subject, so a saturation threshold kept
  85% of it and the palette came back as three greys. The flood-fill mask fixes
  it (subject 29.4% of frame).
- **Colours are pure albedo.** They carry no baked light, so they read flatter
  and darker in a dim preview than the projected maps did, which had the
  concept's highlights baked in. Verified: `#F2A8C4` in, `#F1A6C2` back out of
  the atlas. Do not brighten the palette to compensate for preview lighting;
  brighten the preview.
- `uv_coverage` in the report should match `report.json` from stage 4. On the
  pig both read 0.525, which is the cheap proof that the rasteriser and Blender
  agree about the layout.

**It took three passes on the pig**, each about two minutes: colours too dark
under a dim preview, then the snout too small and the pupils sitting outboard of
the whites, then the brow landing on the ear. That loop is the method, not a
failure of it: paint, render six views, look, adjust three numbers.

#### Projection (`texture_bake.py`, kept, not the default)

Camera-projects the concept onto the mesh. Rebuilt once and it works far better
than it did, but **it still smears** and the failure is structural, not a bug:

- a photograph has to be wrapped around geometry it was never taken of, so
  surfaces edge-on to the projector get colour stretched along the view axis
- only 81% of the pig and 76% of the cow land on the subject at all
- a silhouette cannot tell a view from its mirror, so the last call is always
  yours

Use it when the asset needs the concept's actual markings and a flat palette
would lose them - a specific cow's patches, a decal, a logo. For anything
stylised, paint.

### 5b. The permanent route, verified end to end

Run once when an asset is worth keeping. **Everything here is free**: the Open
Cloud key costs nothing, and Model and Image uploads cost no Robux.

```bash
python scripts/upload_asset.py --file work/out/low.glb   --name Pig_Mesh --asset-type Model
python scripts/upload_asset.py --file work/out/color.png --name Pig_Tex  --asset-type Image
```

Both returned `moderationState: Approved` immediately on a first run.

**THE TRAP THAT COSTS THE MOST TIME HERE: upload the texture as `Image`, NOT
`Decal`.** Both succeed. Both come back Approved. Only one works. A Decal asset
**wraps** an image and has a **different id** from the image inside it, so
assigning a Decal id to `MeshPart.TextureID` **silently does nothing** and the
model renders grey. There is no error anywhere. Measured: the Decal id
left the pig grey; the Image id, from the same PNG,
textured it correctly.

**A .glb uploads as a `Model`, which means there is no bare mesh id to assign.**
The Model wraps a MeshPart. To get a permanent `MeshId` you insert the Model
once and take the MeshPart out of it:

```lua
local m = game:GetObjects("rbxassetid://MODEL_ID")[1]
local p = m:IsA("MeshPart") and m or m:FindFirstChildWhichIsA("MeshPart", true)
p.Parent = workspace
p.TextureID = "rbxassetid://IMAGE_ID"
if m ~= p then m:Destroy() end
```

After this the part carries a real `MeshId` and a real `TextureID`, and survives
saving and publishing.

**IF THE MCP BRIDGE IS WEDGED, USE STUDIO'S COMMAND BAR.** It needs no plugin
and no bridge, and it takes the same Luau. Two things about it:

- **Ctrl+Enter runs it. Plain Enter inserts a newline.**
- Anything touching `CurrentCamera` raises a **"Dangerous Command Detected"**
  dialog that must be cleared before the command runs. Avoid camera calls in an
  automated path, or expect to clear the prompt.

### 5 and 6. Into Studio, with no upload

**This is the finding that unblocked both stages.** The Open Cloud upload needs
`ROBLOX_API_KEY` and the Studio MCP's `upload_decal` needs that or a
`ROBLOSECURITY` cookie. With **neither set**, there is still a complete path:
`AssetService` builds an `EditableMesh` and an `EditableImage` from raw data in
process and hands back a real `MeshPart`.

```bash
# 1. pack the mesh and texture as binary blobs
"$BLENDER" --background \
  --python scripts/export_for_studio.py -- \
  --mesh work/out/low.glb --color work/out/color.png \
  --outdir work/serve --name pig

# 2. serve them to localhost only
python scripts/serve_assets.py --dir work/serve
```

Then run `references/studio_import.lua` through the MCP's `execute_luau`, in
**edit mode**. Measured on the pig: **0.05s** for 5,378 verts, 5,378 UVs, 5,998
triangles and a 1024x1024 texture.

**Three things that were unknown and are now measured:**

- **`HttpService:GetAsync` works from plugin context with
  `HttpService.HttpEnabled = false`.** That setting governs game scripts, not
  plugins. This is what makes the whole route possible.
- **`GetAsync` is byte-exact on a binary body.** A 251,532-byte blob arrived
  intact, so `buffer.fromstring(body)` reads it directly: no base64, no JSON,
  and no giant literal pasted into a script.
- **`CreateMeshPartAsync` is permitted from plugin context in edit mode.** That
  had been an open question here for weeks. It is not.

**THE LIMIT, and it is real.** `MeshContent` and `TextureContent` both come back
as `Enum.ContentSourceType.Object` with a **nil `Uri`**. They are session-local
objects, not asset URIs, so **they will not survive saving or publishing the
place.** This route is for building, iterating and looking at the thing in
engine. Making an asset permanent still needs an upload, or Studio's own
right-click **Save to Roblox** on the resulting MeshPart.

**Two traps, both of which produce a confidently wrong model:**

- **Do not flip the winding when converting axes.** Blender Z-up to Roblox Y-up
  is `(x, y, z) -> (x, z, -y)`, whose determinant is **+1**, so it is a rotation
  and preserves winding. Flipping it "because an axis was negated" renders every
  face backwards: the model looks **hollow and see-through with dark patches**,
  which reads as a texture alpha bug and is not one.
- **Do not flip the texture rows.** Blender's row 0 is the bottom of the image
  and Roblox's buffer row 0 is the top, **but Roblox's UV v also runs from the
  top while Blender's runs from the bottom**. The two conventions cancel, so the
  array is written as-is. Flipping it sends UV islands into the atlas gutter and
  the model comes back **covered in black blotches**. That one cost two wrong
  diagnoses first: texture resolution, then the UV dedupe. Both were fine.

**Diagnosing this class of bug:** the same mesh and the same texture render
correctly in Blender, so when Studio disagrees, the export is wrong, not the
asset. `paint_texture.py`'s `uv_coverage` matching stage 4's `report.json` is the
cheap proof that the UVs themselves are sound.

## Run a whole set

One manifest, eight stages, all resumable: an asset whose output exists is
skipped unless `--force`.

```bash
python scripts/batch.py concepts --outdir work/farm   # 1-2  text -> concept png
python scripts/batch.py sheet    --outdir work/farm   #      LOOK at the gate sheet
python scripts/kaggle_run.py push   --outdir work/farm --slug farm     # 3
python scripts/kaggle_run.py fetch  --outdir work/farm --slug farm
python scripts/batch.py meshes   --outdir work/farm   # 4    -> low.glb + normal
python scripts/batch.py orient   --outdir work/farm   #      LOOK once, whole set
python scripts/batch.py paint    --outdir work/farm   # 4b   spec + colour map
python scripts/batch.py publish  --outdir work/farm   # 5    Open Cloud upload
python scripts/batch.py studio   --outdir work/farm   # 6    emits _studio_wire.lua
```

Then run `_studio_wire.lua` through the Studio MCP's `execute_luau` in edit mode.

**Proven end to end on 2026-08-26** with a cow and a pig, and again on
2026-08-31 with a coin and a trophy: painted, uploaded, inserted, textured,
standing in a place, permanent.

### THERE ARE TWO IDS PER ASSET AND THEY ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE

Open Cloud cannot upload a raw **Mesh**, so stage 5 uploads a **Model**, and that
model *wraps* a MeshPart whose `MeshId` points at an inner Mesh asset Roblox
mints on ingest. `_assets.json` records the **model** id. Measured 2026-08-31:

```
AssetService:CreateMeshPartAsync(model_id) -> "Failed to load mesh asset"
AssetService:CreateMeshPartAsync(mesh_id)  -> OK, exact size
```

Two consequences, and the first one costs an hour if you meet it cold:

**A MeshPart cannot be expressed in a Rojo `.model.json`.** `MeshId` is not
settable by property assignment. Rojo will build the part, apply `TextureID`,
`Size` and `CFrame`, and leave the geometry blank - and the only symptom is the
plugin saying *"Synced, but 1 change failed to apply"* next to a part that looks
like an untextured cube. Do not try to ship meshes through Rojo.

**So there are two real routes, and they suit different jobs:**

| Route | Needs | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `game:GetObjects(model_id)` | Studio (plugin/`execute_luau`) | **shipping.** Bakes the mesh into the place, so the running game needs no network and no moderation round trip. This is what `_studio_wire.lua` does. |
| `AssetService:CreateMeshPartAsync(mesh_id)` | the INNER mesh id | runtime creation in a live server. Yields. |

The inner `mesh_id` is only discoverable by inserting the model once and reading
`.MeshId` off the result, so **record it** alongside the model id rather than
rediscovering it. In a game project that belongs in a `MeshBank.luau` next to the
`SoundBank`, with a `work/meshes/install.lua` doing the insert - the same shape
as the sfx stage, for the same reason: the ids live on disk, the instances live
in the place.

**And re-check orientation when a mesh replaces a primitive.** A Roblox
`Cylinder`'s flat faces are on its LOCAL X and need a 90 degree roll to read as a
coin; a generated coin mesh is already upright on Z, so the same roll lays it
flat on the floor. Carry the corrective CFrame with the part, not in the caller.

**Uploading was never the fragile part.** The pig, the cow, the coin and the
trophy all uploaded first time. Everything above is about getting an uploaded
asset *into the tree*.

### The two stages that need eyes, and why that is not a human clicking

`sheet` and `orient` both produce ONE image for the WHOLE set. The agent reads
them. Nobody has to click anything, and neither is skippable:

- **`sheet`** is the 2D concept gate. It has already caught a bee that generated
  as three bees and a chicken that generated as a grid of seven.
- **`orient`** answers which end of each body axis is the head. **Geometry
  cannot decide this.** The cross-section heuristic is right on a pig (11.3x)
  and **wrong on a cow** (2.3x), because a cow's rump out-bulks its head. Width
  contradicts too, in the opposite direction: the pig's head region is wider
  than its rump, the cow's is narrower. Two animals, two contradictions.
  `make_paint_spec.py` therefore **refuses** to guess below 5x and `batch.py
  paint` **skips** any asset still marked `UNKNOWN` in `_orientation.json`.

Read the orient sheet like this: a **green sphere marks the MAX end** of the
body axis. Head opposite it means `min`; head on the same side means `max`.

### Speed: what is worth optimising, measured

Timed on a desktop CPU with the pig, 2026-08-26. Optimise what is
actually slow, not what feels slow.

| Step | Cost | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `mesh_pipeline` (600k -> 6k + normal bake) | **14.7 s** | the local floor. Cost is welding and decimating 600k faces |
| the same with a **512** bake instead of 1024 | 13.4 s | **not worth it.** Saves 1.3 s and costs texture quality |
| `make_paint_spec` + `paint_texture` | **3.7 s** | painting is nearly free |
| `render_check`, 6 views, **Cycles** | **16.8 s** | was costing 4x the actual work |
| `render_check`, 6 views, **EEVEE** | **6.5 s** | **now the default.** Reads identically for judging placement |
| `render_check`, 6 views, **Workbench** | 3.9 s | fastest, flatter. `--engine WORKBENCH` when you only need placement |

**Two changes came out of this, both real:**

- **EEVEE is the default render engine.** The sheet exists to answer "did the
  colour land in the right place", and EEVEE answers it identically 2.6x faster.
  Cycles is still there with `--engine CYCLES` for a presentable render.
- **`batch.py --jobs N` runs per-asset work in parallel** for `meshes` and
  `paint`. The jobs are genuinely independent. Default is `cores // 3`, because
  Blender is itself multi-threaded and more than that thrashes. Measured on two
  assets: 15.4 s serial, 9.4 s at `--jobs 4`; the gain scales with set size.

**What NOT to touch:**

- **Hi3DGen sampler steps.** That is the quality knob, not a speed knob.
- **Bake resolution.** Measured above: 1.3 s.
- On a real sixteen-asset run the **Kaggle round trip dominates everything
  local** - ~102 GPU-seconds per asset plus kernel boot and dependency install.
  Local Blender work is minutes; the GPU stage is tens of minutes. Push all
  sixteen in ONE kernel run and do the local stages while it is queued.

### The spec generator

`make_paint_spec.py` writes a first-pass paint spec from measured landmarks plus
the concept's palette, so a set of sixteen is not sixteen hand-authored specs.
It reproduced the hand-tuned pig closely enough to be indistinguishable at
gameplay distance.

- **Patterned animals get a patch scatter.** If the palette holds a second
  common colour far from the base in luminance, a deterministic set of patch
  blobs is added. Without it the cow came out **entirely white** - a clean model
  of the wrong animal.
- The scatter is fixed, not random, so a set regenerates identically.
- The generated spec is plain JSON. Move a stamp, change a colour, delete the
  patches - then rerun `paint` with `--force`.

**Always render after painting.** `scripts/render_check.py` gives six views on a
plain ground. The spec generator is a first pass, not an oracle.

## Verify before believing

```bash
"$BLENDER" --background --python scripts/verify.py
"$BLENDER" --background --python scripts/verify_texture.py
```

`verify.py` builds an 82k-triangle high-poly, runs the whole geometry stage on it,
and asserts on the outputs: the split import was detected and welded, triangle
count under budget, UVs exist, lie in range and cover enough of the texture, the
normal map is neither empty nor flat, the exported GLB re-imports at the reported
count. **19 checks.**

`verify_texture.py` uses **Suzanne**, because the test has to be able to fail: a
sphere looks the same from every side, so a view picker would score 100% while
being wrong. It renders her from a known direction as a fake concept and asks the
stage to recover that direction from silhouettes alone, then checks the colour
bake landed. **9 checks.**

**Both suites pass as of 2026-08-24.** They fail loudly rather than exiting 0 on a
broken artifact, which they have already done twice: the flat-normal-map bug in
trap 0 was found by `verify.py` on its first run, and the left/right silhouette
ambiguity by `verify_texture.py` on its first run.

**And then look at the PNG.** The verifier checks that a normal map has variation;
it cannot tell you the seams are ugly. Code exiting 0 is not the artifact being
correct.

## References

- `references/traps.md` - every failure mode found so far, symptom first
- `references/licences.md` - the licence audit, what was read and when
- `scripts/export_for_studio.py` + `scripts/serve_assets.py` + `references/studio_import.lua` - the no-upload route into Studio
- `scripts/make_paint_spec.py` - measured landmarks + palette -> a first-pass spec
- `scripts/orient_sheet.py` - the head-end gate for a whole set in one image
- `scripts/render_check.py` - six views of a textured mesh, for judging by eye
- `scripts/paint_texture.py` - the painter, and `axes_probe.py` for object-space orientation
- `references/example-pig.paint.json` - a hand-tuned spec (solid colour)
- `references/example-manifest.json` - a batch manifest to copy (`--manifest`); names, studs, prompts, optional per-asset `tris`
- `references/example-cow.paint.json` - a GENERATED spec (patterned, patch scatter)
- `scripts/pair_sheet.py` - concept next to the mesh from both sides, the 4b eye check
- `references/kiln-route.md` - HOW: the hard-surface route with Kiln, run end to end to a Roblox-ready GLB
- `scripts/kiln_to_roblox.mjs` - Kiln GLB -> Roblox: -Z front, studs, one mesh per hex-named colour, 20k tri gate
- `references/example-rifle.kiln.js` - a worked hard-surface program
- `references/hard-surface-route.md` - WHY hard surface forks off this pipeline (its the assistant Design route is superseded by Kiln)
- `references/studio-wire.lua` - insert, SurfaceAppearance, CollisionFidelity

## Fallback ladder

| Tier | Route | When |
|---|---|---|
| T3 | Kiln program -> `kiln_to_roblox.mjs` -> Studio Import 3D | **Hard-surface objects.** First choice for them, not a fallback |
| T2 | This pipeline | Default for organic, and for any batch |
| T1 | Studio MCP `generate_mesh` (Cube 3D) | Space down, quota gone, or the clock beat you |
| T0 | Primitive parts assembled in code | Always works, never impressive |

Decide which tier you will drop to before you start a long batch. Deciding mid-run wastes the run.

## Quadrupeds: rig, animate, and export as a SKINNED mesh

Promoted from a real build 2026-09-09. Four-legged creatures are not covered by
the R15 rig, so this chain exists to fit one:

| Script | Does |
|---|---|
| `probe_rig.py` | Report what is actually inside a rigged blend before building on it |
| `quadruped_rig.py` | Fit a 19-bone armature by MEASURING the mesh, then skin it explicitly - Blender's `ARMATURE_AUTO` binds ZERO vertex groups on these meshes, silently, with no error |
| `quadruped_anim.py` | Gaits from footfall phases: walk LATERAL, run DIAGONAL, lunge BOUND |
| `export_skinned.py` | Export a Roblox-ready skinned GLB, and emit each bone's swing axis expressed in its OWN rest basis |

**Export as a skinned mesh, not as one rigid box per bone.** A previous build did
the latter and argued for it - a skinned MeshPart must be uploaded before Roblox
accepts bones, and the run could not verify that round trip. The upload works,
and the performance law it was really defending (no Humanoid, no Animator, one
bulk write per frame) is BETTER served by the mesh: `Bone.Transform` is a plain
property set, and a skinned creature puts ONE part into a `BulkMoveTo` where
nineteen boxes put nineteen.

`export_skinned.py` refuses to ship a mesh Roblox will render wrong: more than 4
influences on any vertex (Roblox silently drops the rest, which reads as a limb
tearing on one animation frame), or any vertex bound to no bone at all. It emits
the swing axis per bone because `Bone.Transform` is expressed in the bone's own
rest frame - a hardcoded X rotation is right for some bones and quietly wrong for
others, which reads as "the walk looks a bit odd" rather than as a bug.

## Mesh verification scripts

| Script | Answers |
|---|---|
| `check_colours.py` | Does the colour map's ACTUAL pixels match the spec hexes? This is the gate for the linear/sRGB trap - a paint pass once shipped every map at half brightness, asking `#969BA0` and writing `#4E545A`, with no metric noticing. Sample the file, never trust the lighting |
| `check_prop.py` | What fraction of a built prop's VISIBLE surface is the thing you meant it to be |
| `landmarks.py` | Dump a mesh's landmarks with the head end STATED, not inferred |
| `zprofile.py` | Per-height slice - how wide is the mesh at each point along its length. Print the whole profile BEFORE writing a rule about its shape; three verifier rewrites came from picking an extreme instead of a landmark |
| `finish_creature.py` | Centre a creature on its own mass, export, and MEASURE the result |

## Tier 3 and measurement scripts

These scripts are the code-authored fallbacks and the batch checks. Each one has a job in the pipeline above.

- `scripts/tier3_props.py`: code-authored stand-ins for props Hi3DGen could not produce (bush, sandwich). Run inside Blender with `--kind`.
- `scripts/grass_clump.py`: a grass clump built from code to meet a scatter budget that the generator cannot meet.
- `scripts/wedge_slice.py`: a fruit or cake wedge (a circular sector, extruded), Tier 3.
- `scripts/measure_set.py`: measures every `<asset>/out/low.glb` in a batch against its brief and prints one table. Use it after a batch so a small budget miss is not hidden.
- `scripts/compare_sheet.py`: renders two colour maps on the same mesh, one row each, with the same views and light. Use it to show a before and after.

ul-animation.text:
---
name: ul-animation
description: Author Roblox character animations (R15 or R6) headlessly in Blender from a JSON pose spec, verify them by rendering contact sheets and GIFs and match a reference pose. Use this whenever the user wants to make, generate, or automate a Roblox animation — a punch, swing, emote, idle, walk, death, tool action — or wants an animation built to match a reference pose, or asks to animate a .blend rig without opening Blender's UI. Also trigger when a Roblox animation "comes apart", limbs detach, a rig poses correctly in script but renders wrong, limbs pop or flip between frames, or a pose looks nothing like the reference.
---

# Roblox animation, headless

> **First time on this machine?** Read `LOCAL.md` in this folder. If it does not exist, run the
> `ul-setup-check` skill (or copy `LOCAL.template.md` to `LOCAL.md` and fill it in).
> `LOCAL.md` holds your paths and tool locations; it is yours and is never shared.

Author animation as **data** (a JSON spec of poses over time), bake it into a real
Blender Action, render it, and **look at the result** before believing it.

The loop is: **author → render every frame → tile into a contact sheet → look →
correct → repeat.** Everything here exists because some step of that loop caught a
failure that every other check missed.

## Read this first: the trap that wastes the most time

**Most Roblox rigs ship a Blender Action holding their rest pose.** Blender
**re-evaluates that Action during render**. So if you set pose values and then
render:

- every numeric probe reports your pose applied perfectly
- every rendered frame shows the rig's default pose
- the data and the image never reconcile, and there is no error

Clearing the Action does not help either, because **that Action IS the rest pose** —
clear it and the limbs collapse into the torso.

**The fix: insert KEYFRAMES into that same Action**, then `frame_set()` per frame
and render. The animation then *is* the Action, nothing can overwrite it, untouched
bones hold their rest values by constant extrapolation, and you end up with a real
Action — which is what a Roblox export needs anyway. `scripts/anim_render.py`
already does this.

Full list in `references/traps.md` — 28 of them. Read it before debugging anything.

## Author in FK. Not IK.

A Roblox `KeyframeSequence` is **a tree of per-joint rotations**, one per Motor6D.
That is FK. Every R15 rig ships one control bone per joint to match. Drive the
character with IK targets and you are round-tripping through a solver Roblox never
asked for, and paying for it:

- **position-only IK targets leave limb ROLL free**, so blocky Roblox parts present
  whatever face the solver picks and snap between frames. On a textured avatar that
  reads as **colours changing instantly** — the symptom that makes an animation look
  buggy
- **the solver hops between equally-good branches** frame to frame, so limbs pop
  while every frame still verifies perfectly
- it is slow

FK has no branches, no singularities, no roll ambiguity, is exactly 1:1 in degrees,
and exports straight to Roblox.

**Most rigs ship in IK mode**, which makes every `FK_*` bone read as inert. Flip the
switch — do not conclude FK is dead:

```json
"properties": {"ARM_IK_FK.L": 0.0, "ARM_IK_FK.R": 0.0,
               "LEG_IK_FK.L": 0.0, "LEG_IK_FK.R": 0.0}
```

Measured on a free community R15 rig, and pleasantly uniform: every limb rests pointing
straight **down**; on every `FK_*` bone **X negative swings forward, Z positive
swings to the character's right**, 1:1 in degrees, **identical on both sides** — no
mirror inversion. Child angles are relative to the parent.

The general lesson, whatever rig you use: **if a control bone is inert, look for a
switch that disables it before writing it off.** Rigify-style R15 rigs carry
`ARM_IK_FK` / `LEG_IK_FK` custom properties that default to `1.0` (IK). Set them to
`0.0`, key them (so `frame_set` cannot flip them back), and author in FK. The
direction conventions above were measured on one rig; `calibrate_rig.py` and
`sweep_control.py` re-measure them on yours, so run them on any rig you have not used.
Your rig's `.blend` path goes in `LOCAL.md`.

Reach for IK only when a limb must hit an exact world point. Then read traps 12–15.

## Make it look like Roblox, not like the reference

- **30 FPS**, and a combat move runs **0.3–0.7s**. The Animation Editor's default is
  30fps. Real-life timing is far too slow for a game. Take
  the **mechanics** from how the move really works; take the **timing** from Roblox.
- **Five poses**: idle, anticipation, contact, follow-through, recovery.
- **Ease per segment** — `"ease": "in"` to accelerate into the strike, `"out"` to
  settle. A fixed smoothstep decelerates into every keyframe, so the strike eases to
  a stop at its own contact frame and the whole thing reads mushy.
- **Exaggerate.** Real Roblox combat animation goes well past human range and reads
  off the silhouette.
- **Render plain grey** (`"plain": true`). A busy avatar texture turns a blocky rig
  into an unreadable jumble and you end up debugging the costume instead of the pose.
  Real Roblox animations are showcased on a plain dummy for exactly this reason.

**`references/pose-recipes.md` has the actual numbers** — measured angle tables for
guard, anticipation, chamber, contact and follow-through, the timing skeleton, and
the two rules that catch people out (shoulder + elbow must stay under ~120 total;
a high kick needs `UpperLeg X` past −120 or the leg merges with the torso). Start
from those and adjust against the preview. Do not re-derive them.

## Be fast — measured, not guessed

The whole loop is **seconds**. If a pass takes minutes, something is wrong.
Measured on a mid-range PC, one animation of 24–36 frames:

| stage | time | notes |
|---|---|---|
| Blender loads the rig | **0.7s** | startup is never the problem |
| numeric probe (whole FK control map) | **0.1s** | ask the rig questions with numbers |
| preview render (`"preview": true`) | **4–6.5s** | 1 view, 320x240, 1 sample |
| full render, 2 views @ 640x560 | **9–17s** | do this once, at the end |
| GIF encode | **0.3s** | |
| `to_roblox.py` → Luau | **0.1s** | |
| build + verify in Studio | **one `execute_luau` call** | |

**Machine time for a finished, in-Studio animation: well under a minute.** What
actually costs time is *authoring iterations*, so spend them on the preview and
never on the full render. With `references/pose-recipes.md` to start from, a
second move should land in 1–3 previews — the punch and the wave in
`references/` were both right on the **first** try.

`"report": true` prints every joint's position at each beat: when a pose looks
wrong it names the joint in one run instead of five render passes of guessing.

**Do not render to answer a question a probe can answer.**

## Non-negotiables

Each is here because skipping it shipped something broken that looked fine:

1. **Never trust a run that exited 0.** `anim_render.py` asserts rig integrity per
   frame, asserts the frames were written, and hard-exits non-zero otherwise.
2. **Look at the frames.** Every pass.
3. **With a reference, build the side-by-side and judge on that** — never on the
   render alone.
4. **Inspect the finished GIF itself**, not the PNGs you encoded it from.
5. **Never relax a tolerance to turn a red light green.** Fix the spec.

## Workflow

### 1. Calibrate the rig (any rig you have not used)

```bash
blender --background <rig>.blend --enable-autoexec --python scripts/calibrate_rig.py
blender --background <rig>.blend --enable-autoexec --python scripts/sweep_control.py -- FK_UpperLeg.R:rot TORSO:rot
```

`calibrate_rig.py` reports the deform vs control armature, the Action trap, the
**IK/FK switch state**, and which controls actually move something.
`sweep_control.py` gives each axis's direction, sign and usable range — it measures
bone *direction* as well as position, so rotation-only controls are not missed.

If the `FK_*` bones read inert, that is the IK/FK switch, not a dead rig.

### 2. Author the spec

`fps`, `duration`, `w`, `h`, `margin`, `views`, `properties`, `plain`, `preview`,
`report`, and `keyframes[]` of `{t, ease, bones: {Bone: {rot|loc|target|aim}}}`.

`rot` is what you want almost always. `loc` for controls with no end effector
(`ROOT`). `target` / `aim` are the IK escape hatch — see traps 12–15.

Three things that go wrong every time if you forget them:

- **FK child angles compound with the parent.** Shoulder 50° + elbow 70° puts the
  forearm 120° from vertical, pointing up over the shoulder. Keep shoulder + elbow
  under ~110° for a guard.
- **Lean and twist go on `UpTorso`**, which drives only the upper body. `TORSO`
  drives the legs too, so leaning it tips the figure over and slides the planted
  foot. The rig also *amplifies*: `X = +15` swings the head 23°.
- **Counter-rotate the support ankle**, `FK_Foot.X ≈ -(FK_UpperLeg.X +
  FK_LowerLeg.X)`, or the foot tilts with the leg and the character looks like it is
  standing on a slope.

See `references/example-fk-roundhouse.json` (0.8s kick) and
`references/example-fk-punch.json` (0.5s cross), plus `references/pose-recipes.md`.

### 2a. IF A PROP IS IN THE HAND, RESEARCH HOW IT IS REALLY HELD. FIRST.

**This step happens BEFORE you author a keyframe, and it is not optional.** The
moment a clip has a weapon or a tool in it, "does the pose read" stops being a
question about the rig and becomes a question about that object, which is a fact
about the world and not something to infer from a matrix.

The failure this exists to prevent, from a real build: a glaive was authored with
its head DOWN at the wielder's hip. Every downstream stage then did its job
perfectly - the engine reproduced the authored grip, the pose strip matched the
contact sheet frame for frame, grip error 0.000, zero samples of the weapon
inside the body - and the game shipped a polearm carried upside down. **A wrong
pose authored here is invisible to every check after it, because every check
after it is measuring agreement with THIS.** When a human finally
looked, the verdict was that it was upside down. They were right, and the cost was
an entire session downstream of a decision made in ten seconds here.

Before authoring:

1. **Search for how the weapon class is carried and used.** Photographs of
   practitioners, not concept art, not other games. Ten seconds of reading beats
   four rounds of guessing at numbers.
2. **Write the answer into the spec as `_intent`,** as a sentence about the
   weapon: "head up, shaft crossing the lead shoulder", "blade angled up and
   forward from a lowered hand". That sentence is what the contact sheet gets
   judged against - see step 4.
3. **Sanity-check the obvious ones from the list below** before reaching for a
   search.

| class | at rest | in a swing |
|---|---|---|
| polearm, glaive, naginata, spear | **head UP** - shouldered, planted butt-to-ground, or at a guard with the blade at chest height or above. Never hanging at the feet | the head leads the arc; the shaft crosses in front of the body, never in the same vertical plane as the arm |
| sword | angled up and forward from a **lowered** hand, around +35 degrees. Straight down reads as dropped | edge leads; the wrist is not a hinge, the whole arm carries the arc |
| axe, hammer | head up or shouldered, the weight carried high | the head is the mass - it arrives last and it arrives hardest |
| fist weapon, gauntlet | worn, not gripped; a brawler's guard, both fists up | the hips drive it, not the shoulder |

**Hold the prop in a pose the wearer's own body could get into.** A one-handed
carry of anything longer than the character is tall does not sit in the same
plane as the arm, or it clips.

### 3. Render and verify

```bash
blender --background <rig>.blend --enable-autoexec --python scripts/anim_render.py -- spec.json out/
ffmpeg -start_number 0 -i "out/side_%03d.png" -vf "scale=240:-1,tile=6x6" sheet.png
```

The camera frames itself on the **whole animation's** bounds and solves its distance
from the field of view, so nothing leaves frame; `margin` (default 1.10) is the only
knob. Render **at least two angles** — a right-leg kick is invisible from the left.

**Then judge the sheet against the REFERENCE, not against itself.** Open the
`_intent` sentence from step 3a and check the sheet frame by frame against it:
is the head up, is the blade leading, does the shaft cross in front of the body.
A contact sheet only ever proves that the render matches the spec. It cannot tell
you the spec was right, and every stage downstream will treat it as ground truth
- so this is the last point in the pipeline where a wrong pose is cheap to fix.
If the sheet and the reference disagree, the reference wins and the spec changes.

### 4. Deliver a GIF, then check the GIF

```bash
ffmpeg -framerate 30 -start_number 0 -i "out/side_%03d.png" -framerate 30 -start_number 0 -i "out/tq_%03d.png" -filter_complex "[0]scale=420:-1[a];[1]scale=420:-1[b];[a][b]hstack=2,split[s0][s1];[s0]palettegen=stats_mode=diff[p];[s1][p]paletteuse=dither=bayer:bayer_scale=3" -loop 0 anim.gif
```

**Read the sheet ONCE, at the size you need and no larger.** A contact sheet is
the most expensive object in this pipeline: an image is re-sent on every later
tool call in the same context, so a full-resolution sheet read early costs
hundreds of thousands of tokens by the end of a run. Tile it down, crop to the
limb in question when that is the question, and do not re-open it to re-check
something you could have measured. Where a check can be a NUMBER - does the
weapon leave the hand, does it pass through a limb, what angle does it sit at -
make it a number and read one line of text instead.

Then pull frames back out of the finished GIF and look at them — motion reads
differently from stills, and encode settings fail silently:

```bash
ffmpeg -i anim.gif -vf "select='not(mod(n,2))',tile=4x3" -vsync 0 verify.png
```

## An authored clip breaks the ones you did not author

Roblox's default `Animate` script plays idle, walk, run, jump, fall and climb at
**Core** priority. Anything you author and play at `Idle` or above **masks them
on every joint it poses**, for as long as it is playing.

So a full-body idle loop - the correct fix for a character standing there with a
weapon - stops the legs from moving when the player walks, because your clip is
posing the legs at a higher priority than the walk cycle. It looks exactly like
"the walk animation is missing", and it appears only on the character you
authored the idle for, which makes it read as a problem with that character's
weapon.

**Pick one and say which:**

- author the idle at **`Core`** priority, so the default walk still wins; or
- **do not pose the legs** in it - author only the arms and torso and let the
  default locomotion drive everything below the hips; or
- **author the locomotion set too** (walk and run at `Movement`), which is the
  only option if the carry pose has to change how the character walks.

**And check it, per character, in a playtest:** stand still, walk, run, jump,
land. Watch the LEGS. This costs about fifteen seconds per fighter and there is
no static check that can see it - the clip is correct, the rig is correct, and
the defect only exists while two clips are playing at once.

## R15 vs R6

**Prefer R15.** R15 has elbows and knees, so it has a joint for every angle a
reference shows, and FK maps one control bone to each.

R6 limbs are **rigid single blocks with no elbow**. A folded boxing guard is not a
pose R6 can hold at all; asking for it raises the whole arm. Use R6 only when the
game requires it, and expect stiff pose-to-pose motion — which is R6's native look,
not a defect.

## Getting it into Roblox — the full pipeline

Verified end to end, and it needs **no upload**.

```bash
# 1. author + preview until it reads right   ("preview": true)
blender --background <rig>.blend --enable-autoexec --python scripts/anim_render.py -- spec.json out/

# 2. generate the Studio builder for one or many specs
python scripts/to_roblox.py kick.json punch.json wave.json > build.lua
```

3. Paste `build.lua` into `execute_luau`. It creates
   `ReplicatedStorage.CustomAnims` with one `KeyframeSequence` per spec, replacing
   any of the same name, then **verifies each one loads at its authored duration**
   and prints a report. Anything other than the durations you authored is a
   failure — do not move on.

4. Copy `references/studio-binder.lua` into a LocalScript under
   `StarterPlayer.StarterPlayerScripts`, edit its `BINDS` table, and you have
   key-triggered animations on the player's character (with respawn handling) and
   optionally mirrored onto a dummy.

Spec fields the exporter reads: `rbx_name` (Studio name), `priority` (default
`Action`, which overrides the stock walk/idle), `loop`.

**No upload:** `KeyframeSequenceProvider:RegisterKeyframeSequence(seq)` returns a
ContentId you assign straight to `Animation.AnimationId`. It needs only the
Animation capability, so a LocalScript can call it at runtime — no asset upload,
no moderation, no account. Only the **bare** string works (`hash://` and
`rbxasset://` both fail). Those ids are **session-local**: fine for testing, but
publishing needs real uploaded asset IDs.

Things that will catch you (details in traps 29–34):

- Modern rigs may carry **`AnimationConstraint`**, not `Motor6D` — 15 of them and
  zero Motor6D. Animations still bind by part name and play unchanged.
- `Enum.PoseEasingStyle` has **no `Quad`** — Linear/Constant/Cubic/Elastic/Bounce.
- You **cannot** preview a pose by writing `.Transform` in edit mode; that is the
  animation channel and only the Animator applies it. Verify the axis map by
  forward kinematics through the attachments instead.
- Studio tooling has blind spots: `capture_screenshot` fails while a script tab is
  showing rather than the 3D viewport, and play-mode output may be unreachable —
  so make the runtime script **diagnose itself on screen**, as the binder does.

Coordinate systems differ: **Roblox is +Y up / −Z forward, Blender is +Z up / −Y
forward.**

## Free library fallback

If authoring is not converging, the Creator Store carries free R15 animations and
`search_asset` finds them — free, pre-licensed, no quota, no upload, no moderation,
and already an Animation asset ID. Under an unattended-agent rule, an agent
searching and selecting is not a human intervention.

## FK solver, probe and example configs

- `scripts/fk_crouch.py`: solves leg angles that keep the feet planted and flat for a crouch or landing squash. Use `--json` for a spec-ready bones block.
- `scripts/fk_probe.py`: probes the community R15 rig in Blender and solves joint angles offline from a JSON input. It is not IK; it is FK by reading the rig.
- `references/example-fk-wave.json` and `references/example-uppercut.json`: example input configs for the FK path (a wave emote and a rear-hand uppercut). Copy one as a starting point for a new clip.

ul-build-orchestrator.text:
---
name: ul-build-orchestrator
description: Runs a Roblox game build pipeline as a timed, logged run (market research, design, code, 3D/materials/UI/animation/VFX/SFX, assembly, playtest, publish), fans the asset block out to subagents while keeping every Studio write on one thread, enforces the write boundary, and keeps a timestamped ledger of stalls, fallbacks and interventions with a debts gate so a run cannot end with known defects. Use this whenever you are running or planning a full Roblox build, want the agent pipeline orchestrated, parallelised, or handed to a manager agent, mention an intervention counter, the 30-minute stall rule, or Tier 2 to Tier 1 fallbacks, or ask whether subagents would help a Roblox build. Also use it to rehearse the roster on a practice run before a build you care about, because an untested orchestration layer is a second variable.
---

# Roblox Build Orchestrator

> **First time on this machine?** Read `LOCAL.md` in this folder. If it does not exist, run the
> `ul-setup-check` skill (or copy `LOCAL.template.md` to `LOCAL.md` and fill it in).
> `LOCAL.md` holds your paths and tool locations; it is yours and is never shared.

Runs a Roblox game build end to end under a wall-clock cap, with a ledger that
doubles as the evidence of how the run went. The pipeline itself (stages, specs,
gates) is defined by the `ul-game-pipeline` skill; this skill times it, logs it,
and decides how the asset block is split across workers. It orchestrates the
stage skills (`ul-3d-model`, `ul-texture-gen`, `ul-ui-builder`,
`ul-animation`, `ul-vfx-library`, `ul-sfx-finder`, `ul-map-builder`); it does not replace them.

## Start here

If you invoke this skill, walk the user through the below and run the commands
for them. Nobody should have to remember any of it.

**Setup.** The worker definitions live in this skill's `agents/` folder and must
be installed where your AI coding tool reads agents. The pack's installer normally does
this. To confirm, or after a machine change:

```bash
mkdir -p agents && cp skills/ul-build-orchestrator/agents/*.md agents/
```

(`ul-agent-map` is the seventh worker; it ships alongside the others in the
pack's `agents/` folder, and the same copy command installs it.)

**Every run, three steps:**

1. **Start the ledger.** `run_log.py init --run <name> --mode fanout`
2. **Run the pipeline**, bracketing each stage and logging every event as it
   happens. Details under *Mode B* below.
3. **Ask for the verdict.** `run_log.py decide`, then `run_log.py debts`.

## The rule that decides the architecture

**Fan out the asset block. Keep the spine on one thread. Measure both.**

The asset block (meshes, materials, UI, animation, VFX, SFX, and the map) is
mutually independent, all downstream of one design spec, and generation-heavy.
That is the shape fan-out is for, and `ul-game-pipeline` runs it that way by
default because of what was measured: the saving is not wall-clock, it is token
cost, in two independent halves. First, every tool call re-sends the whole
conversation, so a long single window costs closer to quadratic than linear, and
images (contact sheets, screenshots) re-send forever; in a worker they stay in the
worker. Second, per-agent model tiering only applies inside a subagent.

The spine is different. Design needs research, code needs design, assembly needs
code and assets, playtest needs assembly. The best controlled evidence on
multi-agent systems (Nature Machine Intelligence 2026, 260 configurations with
compute held constant) found that single-agent baseline performance is the
strongest predictor of whether coordination helps, and that past a capability
threshold extra agents make things *worse*. Anthropic's own multi-agent win is
explained almost entirely by token spend, not by coordination. So the dependent
stages stay on one thread.

Two consequences:

- A practice run **is** the baseline measurement. `run_log.py decide` reads the
  stage timings and tells you whether the split paid off, so the stage
  boundaries can be retuned.
- An untested orchestration layer is a second variable. If a run goes badly you
  cannot tell whether the model failed at making a game or the briefing failed at
  handing out work. Rehearse the roster on a practice run before a build you care
  about.

## Every run: the ledger

A number reconstructed afterwards from memory is not evidence, and the 30-minute
stall rule is the rule most likely to be broken in the moment, so it needs
something outside the moment to enforce it.

Start every run, including a practice run, with:

```bash
python skills/ul-build-orchestrator/scripts/run_log.py init --run <name> --mode fanout
```

Then bracket each stage and log every event as it happens, not afterwards:

```bash
run_log.py start --stage 3d-meshes
run_log.py event --kind fallback --stage 3d-meshes --note "TRELLIS.2 queue 8m, dropped to Cube 3D"
run_log.py end   --stage 3d-meshes --status fell-back
run_log.py status                 # is the current stage past the stall rule
run_log.py counter                # one status line; also written to counter.txt
run_log.py report                 # stage timing table + event lists
run_log.py decide                 # did the fan-out pay off, from what was measured
```

`counter.txt` is a single line that anything can tail (a text overlay, a status
bar, a dashboard), so a live count stays honest without anyone maintaining it by
hand.

### What counts as an intervention

Log the ones that count with `--kind intervention` the moment they happen.

**Free, does not count:** pressing Play, stopping a test, clicking Publish;
restarting a crashed or stuck MCP server; approving a tool call; creating the
universe and place shell once before the run; anything purely mechanical that no
API can reach.

**Counts:** writing or editing any line of code yourself; making a design or art
decision; choosing which sound or animation to use (but the agent searching and
selecting from the Creator Store itself is **not** an intervention); telling it
*what* is wrong rather than *that* something is wrong; choosing between options
it presents; clicking through a third-party plugin GUI on the agent's behalf.

A stall the agent resolves itself is not an intervention. Log it as
`--kind stall` so the report still shows where the time went.

## Mode A: solo (the baseline, and the fallback for small jobs)

One thread runs the whole pipeline in order, calling the existing skills per
stage: `ul-3d-model`, `ul-texture-gen`, `ul-ui-builder`, `ul-animation`,
`ul-vfx-library`, `ul-map-builder`. Use it for a quick prototype, for a single asset
stage, or as the baseline you compare a fan-out run against.

Two mechanical rules make the cap real, in both modes:

- **Stall rule.** If one problem eats 30 minutes, stop working on it, take the
  pre-authorised fallback so the run keeps moving, and log it. Check with
  `run_log.py status` at each stage boundary.

  **It protects the RUN, not the FIX, and those are different things.** The
  fallback is what stops one problem eating the run. It is not permission to
  ship the defect. Every stalled problem is healed before the run is called
  done - always, on every run, with no exception and no mode in which it is
  acceptable to carry it forward.

  Measured in one run: the mesh stage stalled, fell back, and the build shipped
  with Cylinder coins - an incomplete game. The cause was a missing `import os`
  in a vendored repo. One hour, once, and every run afterwards has real meshes.
  Deferring that fix does not save time, it re-spends it on every future run and
  ships a worse game each time.

  **The premise is one prompt equals a full game.** That is incompatible with a
  pipeline carrying defects it has already diagnosed. So a run is not finished
  when the game is built - it is finished when `run_log.py debts` exits clean.
  It gates by default; `--list` prints without gating and is for reading
  mid-run, not for finishing one.

- **Fallbacks are pre-authorised.** Attempt Tier 2 first on animation and SFX,
  then fall back to Tier 1 without asking. An agent stopping to ask permission to
  fall back is an intervention caused by an incomplete brief, which is a
  self-inflicted tick on the counter.

At the end, run `run_log.py decide`.

## Mode B: fan-out (the default for the asset block)

Fan out **the asset block only**: map, 3D meshes, materials, UI, animation, VFX,
SFX. Those are mutually independent, all downstream of the one design spec, all
generation-heavy, and each already produces a file. That is the shape fan-out is
for.

Market research can also fan out (independent genre candidates, breadth-first,
one synthesis at the end), and it is the safest place to rehearse the pattern
because nothing it does touches Studio.

**Do not fan out the spine.** Design needs research, code needs design, assembly
needs code and assets, playtest needs assembly. Anthropic names dependency-heavy
work as the poor-fit case explicitly, and adds that coding tasks have fewer
genuinely parallel parts than research does.

### The write boundary is the hard constraint

The Roblox DataModel is single shared mutable state. Two agents doing
`execute_luau` concurrently is the conflicting-writes failure in its purest form,
and it is a failure shape that has already happened twice in practice: the
robloxstudio-mcp duplicate-server timeout deadlock, and the Rojo double-connection
duplicates that killed every Knit controller. Exactly one MCP server is the rule.

So:

- **Workers write files to disk and nothing else.** Meshes, `.model.json`,
  KeyframeSequence specs, audio files, texture maps. No Studio tools at all.
- **One thread does every `execute_luau`, `insert_asset`, assembly, and publish.**

This costs nothing to adopt because the existing skills already emit files rather
than mutating Studio directly. It is enforced by the tool allowlist in each
worker definition, not by asking politely, because a prompt does not reliably hold
a boundary and an allowlist does.

### The roster

Installed at `agents/` (see *Start here*). Works identically in the
your AI coding tool terminal and the desktop app, since both read the same directory.

| Worker | Model | Writes | Tools |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ul-agent-map` | opus | map spec outputs, proven layout, build artifacts | file ops, Bash, no Studio |
| `ul-agent-mesh` | opus | mesh files + manifest | file ops, Bash, no Studio |
| `ul-agent-ui` | opus | `.model.json` + Luau + PNG mockup | file ops, Bash, no Studio |
| `ul-agent-animation` | opus | KeyframeSequence spec + verification renders | file ops, Bash, no Studio |
| `ul-agent-vfx` | opus | VFX kit + manifest, from your harvested library | file ops, Bash, no Studio |
| `ul-agent-sfx` | haiku | audio files + licence note | file ops, Bash, WebFetch, no Studio |
| `ul-agent-market-scout` | haiku | one findings file per genre | read-only + web, no writes to the build |

The tiering rule: **if a human will LOOK AT what the worker produces, the worker
has to be able to judge it.** Gates catch categorical failures, not quality, and
the saving comes from images staying inside the worker, so a worker that cannot
judge its own render has to ship it to the parent, which re-imports the cost the
split was buying. Sound stays on haiku because nothing in this pipeline can hear;
market research stays cheap because it gathers and cites.

Each is read-only with respect to Studio by construction. `maxTurns` on each one
enforces the 30-minute stall rule mechanically rather than by watching a timer.

## Briefing a worker

Workers start cold. They see none of this conversation. An underspecified brief is
the top cause of duplicated work and skipped verification, and every resulting
stall is a tick on the counter.

Every brief carries four fields. The stop condition is the one most often left off
and the one that matters most on a clock.

```
OBJECTIVE   One self-contained outcome. Not a share of a goal you can see and it cannot.
OUTPUT      Exact files, exact paths, exact manifest shape. So the result merges without re-reading.
TOOLS       Which skill, which sources, which tier to attempt first.
BOUNDARIES  What is out of scope, the Tier 2 to Tier 1 fallback (pre-authorised),
            and the wall-clock stop. Report partial work rather than overrunning.
```

Worked examples for the workers, with the exact manifest shapes the assembly
thread expects, are in `references/stage-briefs.md`. Read that before the first
fan-out run rather than improvising briefs on the day.

## What the manager keeps

Never delegated, for the same reason the writes are not:

- The design spec and every design or art decision.
- Verification of every worker report against the artifact it points at. A worker
  saying a mesh is under budget is a claim, not a fact.
- All Studio interaction, assembly, playtest, and publish.
- The ledger.

When two workers disagree, check the artifact rather than averaging the reports.

## Ending a run

```bash
run_log.py report      # the stage table and the full event history
run_log.py decide      # did the fan-out pay off, from what was measured
run_log.py debts       # GATES. The run is not finished until this is clean.
```

**`debts` gates by default and is the step that stops a run being a diary.**
It exits non-zero while any debt is open or closed at doc level only, so a run
cannot quietly end unhealed. Measured: a ledger recorded seven fallbacks and two
stalls faithfully and in real time, and then nothing turned a single one into a
fix. They were fixed hours later because a human asked why they had not been fixed
- not because anything surfaced them.

That is a predictable failure of every honest log: **recording an issue feels
like handling it.** The stall rule deliberately says MOVE ON, which is correct
during a timed run and wrong forever. The debt is real and it comes due on the
next run, unfixed.

So after `debts`, work the list, and pick the STRONGEST fix each one allows:

| | Fix | Property |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **code fix** | the defect becomes unrepresentable. Cannot regress |
| 2 | **gate** | it can still happen, but fails loudly and early |
| 3 | **doc / note** | a future session is told, if it reads it |

**A gate is only real once it has FAILED on a known-bad input.** An untested gate
is a comfort, not a check. And anything left at 3 that could have been 1 or 2
will happen again.

Then write the outcome into your own project notes. The stage timings are the
input to the next run's decision, so they are worth keeping even when the run
went fine.

If this was a practice run and `decide` says the split paid off, rehearse the
roster once more before a run that matters.

## Files in this skill

- `scripts/run_log.py` - the ledger, counter, stall check, timing report, fan-out
  verdict and debts gate. Run `--help` for the full CLI.
- `agents/*.md` - the worker definitions, tool-restricted by construction.
- `references/stage-briefs.md` - worked briefs and manifest shapes per stage.
- `references/write-boundary.md` - why the single-writer rule exists, with the
  failures that motivated it.
- `LOCAL.template.md` - the machine-specific settings (copy to `LOCAL.md`).

ul-check-suite.text:
---
name: ul-check-suite
description: Check Suite for Roblox work - one gate for both Check-UI (screens, buttons, windows, HUDs, menus; 13 rules, Shop, Codes, Rebirth, Settings and Daily Rewards archetypes, GothamBlack, slate canvas, responsive UIScale) and Check-Code (Luau scripts, modules, remotes, DataStore, Config, cleanup; 18 rules). Use on every UI change and every Luau change, and whenever someone asks whether UI or code is finished. Writes one table with PASS, FAIL, WARN, NOT APPLICABLE or UNVERIFIED, and runs check_code.py.
---

# Check Suite - one gate for UI and code

One standard, one gate, one table. Part 1 is Check-UI (every screen, button, window, HUD and menu).
Part 2 is Check-Code (every Luau script, module, remote, data change and Config change).

## The gate (mandatory, no exceptions)

1. For UI, build from the Check-UI modules or the closest example, then check UI-1 to UI-13.
   For code, check CODE-1 to CODE-18 for every changed file.
2. Write one Check Suite table. Use the row labels UI-1 to UI-13 and CODE-1 to CODE-18 so they cannot clash.
   Each row: label, PASS / FAIL / WARN / NOT APPLICABLE / UNVERIFIED, where (file:line, or screen and part), and a note.
3. Run `check_code.py` on changed Luau files when you can, and paste its table in. Run the gui-verify numbers for
   screens. Take screen captures when Studio is present, at a phone size and a PC size if the window can be resized.
4. A FAIL in either part means the item is not done. WARN items must be fixed or explained.
5. Anything that could not be checked is UNVERIFIED, and the report says what the user must run or look at.

A UI or code answer without the Check Suite table is incomplete.

## Part 1 - Check-UI — Clean Roblox UI Design System & Implementation Skill

### 1. Skill Overview & Purpose

**Check-UI** is the definitive design system standard for modern Roblox cartoon, simulator, and tycoon games (inspired by top-tier titles like Pet Simulator 99, Anime Champions, and Blade Ball).

This skill equips any AI agent or human developer with the exact mathematical proportions, color formulas, component architectures, Luau implementations, and responsive scaling mechanisms required to produce pixel-perfect, cohesive, and non-generic Roblox interfaces.

### Core Tenets (Non-Negotiable Rules)
1. **Zero AI Slop / Generic Looks**: Every frame must have intentional cartoon depth, high-contrast borders, pastel highlight strokes, and tactile micro-interactions.
2. **Strict Typography**: Every title, label, counter, button, and text box **must** use `Enum.Font.GothamBlack` with black outline `UIStroke` (thickness proportional to font size: 2.0px to 3.5px).
3. **Solid Canvas (`#3b5866`)**: Never make window backgrounds semi-transparent. Always use solid slate blue `Color3.fromRGB(59, 88, 102)` with `UICorner` (4px) and outer `UIStroke` (3.5px, `#181e22`).
4. **Signature 3D Beveled Square Close Button `[X]`**: Exact 38x38px square with a dark burgundy bottom bevel extrusion (`#730010`), shifted face with vibrant crimson/pink gradient (`#ff7daf` to `#ff1428`), inner pastel stroke highlight, GothamBlack "X", and centered `UIScale`.
5. **2-Tier 3D Header Shadow Divider**: Every header must end with a 2-line separator: an upper 3px dark thematic accent bar + a lower 3px solid black bar.
6. **Seamless Checkerboard (Damier) Fade**: Full-height texture overlay (`rbxassetid://385956923`) with a vertical `UIGradient` transparency sequence (`1 -> 0.82 -> 0.35 -> 0.10`) to eliminate hard cutoff lines.
7. **Aspect Ratio Preservation**: Icons must **never** be stretched. Always set `ScaleType = Enum.ScaleType.Fit`.
8. **Universal Responsive Scaling**: All modal windows and HUDs must be governed by dynamic `UIScale` responsive calculations based on `camera.ViewportSize` (baseline `1050 x 620`, clamped `[0.52, 1.18]`).
9. **Center-Anchored Interactions**: ALL hover, click, and scale animations MUST originate from the exact geometric center via `AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)` + child `UIScale`.
10. **The 5 Canonical Menu Archetypes**: All game interfaces should follow one of the 5 canonical specifications: Shop, Codes, Rebirth, Settings, or Daily Rewards.
11. **Iconless Button Mandate**: Whenever a button WITHOUT an icon is requested (Throw, Action, Jump, Redeem, Confirm, etc.), it MUST ALWAYS strictly follow the Studio-Verified Canonical Standard: sharp 90° rectangular geometry (no UICorner), 3px solid `#0C141A` outer border, 90° color gradient, black checkerboard overlay (`0.91 -> 0.62` fade), TRIPLE glass specular inner highlight frames (`InnerHighlight1`, `2`, `3`), and centered GothamBlack white text with 3px `#11171A` contextual stroke & 1px optical offset.

```lua
    textStroke.Parent = label

    -- 6. Center-Anchored ButtonScale for 4-State Micro-Interactions
    local bScale = Instance.new("UIScale")
    bScale.Name = "ButtonScale"
    bScale.Scale = 1
    bScale.Parent = btn

    return btn
end
```

---

### 4. Multi-Device Responsive Scaling Engine

```lua
local camera = workspace.CurrentCamera

local function getDeviceScale()
    local viewport = camera.ViewportSize
    if viewport.X <= 0 or viewport.Y <= 0 then return 1 end
    -- Baseline resolution: 1050 x 620
    local scaleX = viewport.X / 1050
    local scaleY = viewport.Y / 620
    local factor = math.min(scaleX, scaleY)
    -- Clamped between 0.52 (smartphones) and 1.18 (desktop)
    return math.clamp(factor, 0.52, 1.18)
end

local function updateAllDeviceScales()
    local currentScale = getDeviceScale()
    for _, gui in ipairs(playerGui:GetChildren()) do
        if gui:IsA("ScreenGui") then
            for _, frame in ipairs(gui:GetChildren()) do
                local sc = frame:FindFirstChild("WindowScale")
                if sc and sc:IsA("UIScale") and frame.Visible then
                    sc.Scale = currentScale
                end
            end
        end
    end
end

camera:GetPropertyChangedSignal("ViewportSize"):Connect(updateAllDeviceScales)
```

---

### 5. Center-Anchored Animation Rules & Micro-Interactions

### 5.1 The Center-Anchor Mandate
ALL interactive elements MUST use `AnchorPoint = Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5)`. Scaling then animates uniformly from the visual center.

```lua
local function bindButtonAnimations(btn, scaleObj, hoverFactor, clickFactor)
    assert(btn.AnchorPoint == Vector2.new(0.5, 0.5),
        "[Check-UI] Button '" .. btn.Name .. "' must have AnchorPoint (0.5, 0.5)!")

    local tweenInfoHover = TweenInfo.new(0.08, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
    local tweenInfoClick = TweenInfo.new(0.05, Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)
    local tweenInfoRelease = TweenInfo.new(0.12, Enum.EasingStyle.Back, Enum.EasingDirection.Out)

    btn.MouseEnter:Connect(function()
        playSound(hoverSound)
        TweenService:Create(scaleObj, tweenInfoHover, { Scale = hoverFactor or 1.05 }):Play()
    end)
    btn.MouseLeave:Connect(function()
        TweenService:Create(scaleObj, tweenInfoHover, { Scale = 1.0 }):Play()
    end)
    btn.MouseButton1Down:Connect(function()
        playSound(clickSound)
        TweenService:Create(scaleObj, tweenInfoClick, { Scale = clickFactor or 0.94 }):Play()
    end)
    btn.MouseButton1Up:Connect(function()
        TweenService:Create(scaleObj, tweenInfoRelease, { Scale = hoverFactor or 1.05 }):Play()
    end)
end
```

---

### 6. Continuous Rotating Sunbursts

```lua
local SUNBURST_SPEED = 20 -- degrees per second
RunService.RenderStepped:Connect(function(dt)
    if modalWindow.Visible then
        local delta = SUNBURST_SPEED * dt
        for _, sb in ipairs(sunbursts) do
            sb.Rotation = (sb.Rotation + delta) % 360
        end
    end
end)
```

---

### 7. CheckUIIcons — Production HD Icon Registry (1,022 Icons)

Check-UI ships with **1,022 production-grade HD icons (256px)** pre-uploaded as `rbxassetid://` across 10 categories:
- **Animal** (12), **Currency** (110), **Exclusive** (32), **Food** (48), **Item** (326), **Main** (236), **Nature** (86), **Player** (74), **Social** (24), **UI** (74).

```lua
local CheckUIIcons = require(game.ReplicatedStorage.CheckUI.CheckUIIcons)

-- Direct lookup
local cash = CheckUIIcons.Currency.Cash.Golden_Cash_1st
local player = CheckUIIcons.Player.Player.Player_1st

-- Path lookup
local sword = CheckUIIcons.Get("Item/Sword/Sword 1st")

-- Fuzzy search
local results = CheckUIIcons.Search("diamond")
```

---

### 8. Implementation Checklist

When building any Check-UI interface:
- [ ] **Font**: ALL text uses `Enum.Font.GothamBlack` — no exceptions
- [ ] **Canvas**: Window background is solid `#3B5866` with `BackgroundTransparency = 0`
- [ ] **Close Button**: Uses the exact 38x38 3D beveled square recipe from §3.1
- [ ] **Header Divider**: 2-tier shadow (thematic dark line 3px + pure black 3px)
- [ ] **Damier**: Full-height with 4-point vertical `UIGradient` (no horizontal cutoffs)
- [ ] **Icons**: `ScaleType = Enum.ScaleType.Fit` — never stretched
- [ ] **AnchorPoints**: ALL interactive elements use `AnchorPoint = (0.5, 0.5)` with centered `UIScale`
- [ ] **Button State Triad**: Uses the appropriate color/bevel for `Claim` (Lime), `Claimed` (Silver), `Locked` (Red)
- [ ] **Responsive**: Governed by dynamic `UIScale` based on `ViewportSize` [0.52, 1.18]
- [ ] **Sunbursts**: Rotating at 20°/sec, paused when hidden
- [ ] **Bevels**: 3px dark bottom extrusion on all buttons

## Part 2 - Check-Code (Roblox Luau standard)

Check-Code is the code counterpart of Check-UI. Each rule is short, testable and has a reason.
A piece of code is done only when every rule is PASS or NOT APPLICABLE, and every rule that could not be
checked is written down as UNVERIFIED.

### The gate

1. Read the change, file by file. For each file, go through rules 1 to 18 in order.
2. Write the Check-Code table (format below). Each row: rule, PASS / FAIL / WARN / NOT APPLICABLE / UNVERIFIED,
   and the file and line that shows it.
3. If `check_code.py` can run (see below), run it on the changed files and copy its table into your report.
   Its results count. Do not argue with a FAIL from the scanner. Fix it, or explain why the rule does not apply.
4. Fix every FAIL and run the table again. A change with any FAIL is not done.
5. WARN items are not blockers, but each one must be fixed or named in the report with a reason.
6. Where the project has `ul-luau-code` gates (rojo build, lune test, selene, stylua), run those too.
7. In Studio, when the tools are present: run the change with `execute_luau` only if it is safe (no DataStore
   writes, no reward changes), then read `get_console_output` after a `start_stop_play` run. Report what it showed.

### The rules

1. **Server owns state.** Any change to health, currency, score, inventory, rewards, spawning or purchases is
   decided on the server. A client value is a request, never a fact.
2. **Every remote handler validates.** Check, in order: type, range, ownership, then cooldown or distance.
   Only after all four does the server act.
3. **No deprecated globals.** Use `task.wait`, `task.spawn`, `task.delay`. Never `wait()`, `spawn()`, `delay()`.
   Use `os.clock()` for timing in new code, not `tick()`.
4. **Every `WaitForChild` has a timeout** and handles `nil`. A wait with no timeout can hang forever.
5. **Every lookup is nil-checked** before it is indexed: `FindFirstChild`, `GetService` on a fallible name,
   DataStore reads, `Players:GetPlayerFromCharacter`, any value that can be `nil`.
6. **Every connection has an owner.** Each `:Connect` is stored and disconnected when its owner ends, or the
   code says why it lives forever (for example, a server-wide `PlayerAdded`). See the `lifecycle-cleanup` skill.
7. **No hidden loops.** Every `while true do` has a `task.wait` in it, a way to stop, and a stop when its owner ends.
8. **No per-frame waste.** Code in `Heartbeat`, `PreSimulation`, `PostSimulation` or `RenderStepped` does no
   allocation of tables or closures, no `GetService` or `FindFirstChild` lookups, and no whole-world scans.
   Cache them outside the loop.
9. **DataStore is safe.** Read-modify-write uses `UpdateAsync`, not `GetAsync` then `SetAsync`. Every call is in
   `pcall` with retry and backoff. A failed load never writes defaults over real data.
10. **Remotes match at every end.** Each remote name is defined once (the Net module). The sender, the server
    handler and the receiver use the same argument count and types.
11. **Tunables live in Config.** Balance numbers (prices, health, speeds, timers, spawn rates, sizes) come from a
    Config table. A number in a service body is a FAIL unless it is a structural constant, such as an index or a
    pixel offset, and the code says so.
12. **Every `pcall` reports its error.** `pcall` that discards the error is a FAIL. Capture it and `warn` it, or
    return it to the caller.
13. **Pure logic is pure.** Calculations live in Core modules that take plain numbers and tables, with no
    Instance, service or remote calls, so they can be tested without Studio.
14. **Typed where it counts.** New modules use `--!strict` when the project allows it. Remote payloads and shared
    data shapes have an `export type`. Casts with `::` have a comment saying why they are safe.
15. **No invented APIs.** Every Roblox or Luau call in the change has a line in the API table with its docs page
    and signature, or is marked `-- UNVERIFIED: <API name>`. Memory is not a source.
16. **Clients do not write server state.** A client script never sets a server-owned attribute, value, or
    position that changes gameplay. Attributes that the server sets are read-only on the client by convention.
17. **Effects cannot break gameplay.** Visual and sound code is wrapped so its failure cannot stop a gameplay path.
18. **No leftovers.** No `print` debugging, no commented-out code, no unused locals, no globals created by
    accident. Selene and the scanner check these; a human checks the rest.

### API table (part of the report)

| API | Docs page read | Signature used | Side (server / client / both) |
|---|---|---|---|

Any row missing a docs page is UNVERIFIED, and every use of it is marked in the code.

### Table format

| # | Rule | Result | Where (file:line) | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Server owns state | PASS | Services/Reward.luau:12 | |

### What the scanner can and cannot do

`check_code.py` is a pattern scanner. It finds rule 3 (deprecated globals), rule 4 (WaitForChild with no timeout),
rule 5 (indexing a `FindFirstChild` result on the same line), rule 7 (`while true` with no wait nearby), rule 9
(`GetAsync` and `SetAsync` in one file), rule 12 (`pcall` with no capture), rule 18 (`print`, unused-looking
leftovers, `tick()`), and rule 14 (missing `--!strict`). It does not parse Luau, so it cannot prove rules 1, 2, 6,
8, 10, 11, 13, 15, 16 or 17. Those need a human or the model reading the code, and the table must say so.
A scanner PASS does not mean the code works. Say "passes Check-Code scan" and nothing more.

ul-game-pipeline.text:
---
name: ul-game-pipeline
description: Take a Roblox game from a genre to something built, assembled, playable and published, ONE SECTION PER SESSION - research and plan, code, art, animation and sound, playtest, publish - with a HANDOFF.md between sessions so the chat can be cleared after each approved section. Drives the whole toolchain - market research, a design contract, the code project, map, meshes, textures, UI, animation, VFX and sound, then assembly in Studio, playtest and publish. This is the FRONT DOOR: it owns research, design and assembly itself and delegates each asset stage to the skill that already proves that stage. Use whenever the user wants a Roblox game made, built, started or prototyped, says "make me a game" or names a genre to build (incremental, battlegrounds, ...), asks to "complete the research and plan stage" or any other stage, says "continue with the development of the <genre> game", approves a finished stage ("approved", "looks good"), or asks what is still missing before a game can be built.
---

# Make a Roblox game, end to end

> **First time on this machine?** Read `LOCAL.md` in this folder. If it does not exist, run the
> `ul-setup-check` skill (or copy `LOCAL.template.md` to `LOCAL.md` and fill it in).
> `LOCAL.md` holds your paths and tool locations; it is yours and is never shared.

## START HERE. EVERY RUN IS ONE SECTION PER SESSION. THIS IS THE DEFAULT.

A game is built in six sections. You approve each one, then **clear the chat**
before the next. So the first thing the agent does, before reading further, is
map the prompt to a command and run it:

| You say | The agent runs first |
|---|---|
| "complete the research and plan stage" (optionally naming a genre) | `section.py brief "research and plan"` - a NEW game, section 1 |
| "complete the <art / code / sound / ...> stage" | `section.py resume --game "<words from the prompt>" --expect <that section>` |
| "continue with the development of the incremental game" | `section.py resume --game "continue with the development of the incremental game"` |
