`listed_duration` so that nothing downstream can mistake it for data, and
`pick.py` records `listing_was_wrong` on any pick where the two disagreed by
more than 25%. On the first real run that fired on 2 of 8.

---

## Two Studio calls, never one

`execute_luau` drops all output if the script yields at all, and a Sound does not
resolve its length in the frame you set `SoundId`. So the probe is split:

```
call 1   probe.lua    creates every candidate Sound, returns immediately
         (a beat)
call 2   report.lua   returns role,id,loaded,length as CSV
```

If anything is still `loaded=false` in call 2, run `report.lua` **once more**
before believing it. Only a second failure is a real one, and a real one means
an unresolvable id, a deleted asset, or audio this place is not permitted to use.

---

## The three gates

A candidate is only eligible once Studio says all three, in order:

1. **`IsLoaded == true`** — the id resolves and the place may use it
2. **`TimeLength > 0`** — a zero-length sound is broken, not short
3. **`min_len <= TimeLength <= max_len`** — the role's band

Search score breaks ties, and only ties. A top-ranked listing that fails a gate
always loses to a bottom-ranked one that passes. On the first run this rejected
a 6.55s "wooden gate open" from a role whose band ended at 5s.

**An unfilled role is a failure, not a warning.** `emit_bank.py` refuses to emit
a bank with holes; overriding needs an explicit `--allow-holes`, which means
deliberately shipping a silent event.

---

## Writing a spec

One entry per thing the game needs a sound **for**, never per sound you imagine.

```json
{
 "name": "farm",
 "roles": [
  { "name": "sheep_bleat", "query": "sheep bleat", "kind": "SoundEffect",
    "min_len": 0.3, "max_len": 4.0, "volume": 0.5 },
  { "name": "ambience",    "query": "countryside ambience", "kind": "Music",
    "min_len": 20, "max_len": 300, "volume": 0.2, "looped": true }
 ]
}
```

- `kind` is `SoundEffect` or `Music`. It is a real field on the asset and a
  mismatch is scored down hard, because a Music track answering a `SoundEffect`
  role is the classic way a nine-minute remix ends up as a footstep.
- The band is the design decision. A footstep over 1.5s is not a footstep, and
  writing that down is what lets the machine reject without hearing anything.
- `volume` and `looped` travel through to the emitted bank.

An example spec is in `examples/spec.example.json`; copy it and edit the roles.

---

## Run it

```bash
cd skills/ul-sfx-finder
python scripts/find_sfx.py spec examples/spec.example.json --out work/candidates.json --per-role 5
python scripts/emit_probe.py work/candidates.json --out work
# execute_luau work/probe.lua      -> "created N sounds across M roles"
# execute_luau work/report.lua     -> save the return value verbatim to work/report.txt
python scripts/pick.py work/candidates.json work/report.txt --out work/manifest.json
python scripts/emit_bank.py work/manifest.json --out work
# execute_luau work/install.lua    -> SoundService.SFX, audible in this place
# execute_luau work/tour.lua       -> plays the whole bank in order, so a human can judge it
```

A one-off lookup, no spec needed:

```bash
python scripts/find_sfx.py search --query "wolf howl" --kind SoundEffect --limit 20
```

---

## What ships

| File | Goes to | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `SoundBank.luau` | `src/shared/Config/` | Data only: role -> id, measured length, volume, looped, credit |
| `Sfx.luau` | `src/shared/` | `Sfx.play(role, parent, pitchVary)`, `Sfx.preload()`, `Sfx.stop()` |
| `install.lua` | `execute_luau` | Builds `SoundService.SFX` directly, for a place with no Rojo sync |
| `tour.lua` | `execute_luau` | Plays every sound in order, spaced by its real length |

Two rules the emitted code keeps:

- **Nothing outside the bank ever names an asset id.** Gameplay code says
  `Sfx.play("wolf_howl", head)`. Retuning volume or swapping an asset is a data
  edit, never a code edit.
- **Sound can never break gameplay.** Every entry point in `Sfx.luau` is
  pcall-isolated and returns nil on failure. A missing sound must not stop a shot
  from firing or a sheep from moving.

`tour.lua` schedules with `task.delay` rather than looping with `task.wait`, for
the same reason the probe is split in two: a yielding script loses its output.

---

## Traps

**The listing duration is wrong.** Covered above. It is the single most likely
thing to make this pipeline ship a bad sound if someone "optimises" the Studio
round trip away.

**`search_assets` on the MCP is a dead end.** It returns HTTP 403 `Scope not
authorized`, and no renaming of parameters fixes it. That is why this skill goes
straight to the toolbox endpoints, which need no auth at all.

**You cannot hear anything, and neither can the model.** `assetdelivery` is 401
without a cookie, so there is no waveform, no spectrogram, no loudness figure.
Everything this skill claims about a sound comes from the listing or from
`TimeLength`. When taste matters, run `tour.lua` and let a human judge. For an
unattended run, the gates plus the score are the honest ceiling, and that is a
finding worth saying out loud rather than papering over.

**Free packs are not the same as free audio.** A free Creator Store *pack* is not
loadable until a human takes it into the account (learned the hard way on the VFX
harvester). Individual audio assets used by id have no such step, which is exactly
why this skill works by id and never asks anyone to take anything.

**Volume 0 during probing is deliberate.** 40 candidate sounds resolving at once
in an open Studio would be unpleasant. `probe.lua` sets `Volume = 0`;
`audition.lua`, `install.lua` and `tour.lua` set the real volume.

**Roblox's own stock library scores a deliberate bonus.** Creator id 1 assets
(the `91207…`-shaped ids) are consistent, always permitted and never deleted. If
a run must be reproducible months later, prefer them.

---

## Why library selection and not generated audio

Selecting from the library needs no quota, no ID verification, no moderation
wait and no upload, and an agent searching and selecting from the Creator Store
needs no human intervention.

Generated audio would burn a create-only upload quota to produce something no one
in the loop can hear. That trade is not worth making, and this skill is the
argument.

ul-texture-gen.text:
---
name: ul-texture-gen
description: Generate free AI textures/skins (camo, gold plated, carbon fiber, rust, etc.) for Roblox game assets like guns, weapons, tools, or any part/mesh, and apply them automatically inside Roblox Studio through the official Roblox Studio MCP — no manual clicking through Studio's Texture Generator plugin required. Use this whenever the user wants to texture, skin, retexture, or reskin a Roblox model/mesh/gun/weapon/part, asks for an AI-generated texture or decal for a Roblox object, or wants to automate the Studio texture workflow end-to-end. Also trigger if the user asks for "free" or "no-cost" image/texture generation in a Roblox context, even if they don't name a specific tool. Requires the Roblox Studio MCP connected with Studio open — if that's not available, say so clearly instead of guessing.
---

# Roblox Texture Gen

> **First time on this machine?** Read `LOCAL.md` in this folder. If it does not exist, run the
> `ul-setup-check` skill (or copy `LOCAL.template.md` to `LOCAL.md` and fill it in).
> `LOCAL.md` holds your paths and tool locations; it is yours and is never shared.

This skill is a scriptable texture pipeline: generate a tileable image with a free
API, upload it as an image asset, and write it onto the target part from code. It
works on any part or mesh and batches across a whole model.

The official Studio MCP also has `generate_texture`, which re-textures one MeshPart
or Model in place from a text prompt using Roblox's own AI. Use that when the user
wants a mesh-conforming texture on a single mesh; use this pipeline for tileable
materials, decals, many parts at once, or a texture you want as a reusable file.

## Why this sequence

1. **Image generation happens outside Roblox entirely.** [Pollinations.ai](https://gen.pollinations.ai)
   is a free, keyless image API — a plain HTTP GET returns a PNG. No Studio plugin, no
   paid tier, no signup required (registering is optional and only raises the rate
   limit / drops the watermark).
2. **Roblox only accepts assets it has ingested**, so the generated image has to be
   uploaded as an image asset before anything in Studio can reference it. That's what
   the MCP's `upload_image` is for.
3. **Applying it is just a property write**, done with `execute_luau` (one part or a
   loop over every part of a model).

## Step-by-step

### 0. Check the Studio connection

The tools come from the official Roblox Studio MCP (`list_roblox_studios`,
`get_studio_state`, `search_game_tree`, `inspect_instance`, `execute_luau`,
`upload_image`, `screen_capture`). If they are deferred, load them in one ToolSearch
call. Call `list_roblox_studios` to get the `studio_id` every other call needs, then
`get_studio_state`. If either fails, **stop and tell the user plainly**: the Studio MCP
isn't connected or Studio isn't open. Don't fabricate a result; this pipeline is dead
without a live Studio session.

### 1. Nail down what to generate

Ask (or infer from context) two things if they're not already clear:
- **Style** — e.g. "digital camo", "gold plated brushed metal", "carbon fiber weave",
  "battle-worn rust". Vague requests like "make it cool" are worth a quick clarifying
  question since the result is hard to undo once applied.
- **Target** — the exact part/mesh/model name in the place (e.g. `Handle`, `GunBody`,
  a whole `Model` with multiple parts). Use `search_game_tree` or `inspect_instance` to confirm the name
  exists before generating anything — don't guess a part name and find out it's wrong
  after the image is already made.

Build the generation prompt yourself: append `, seamless tileable texture, flat lighting,
no watermark, high detail` to whatever style the user described — this consistently
produces something closer to a usable game texture than the bare style words alone,
since generic prompts tend to come back as an illustration rather than a tileable
material.

### 2. Generate the image

Run the bundled script rather than hand-rolling the HTTP call — it handles URL encoding,
retries on Pollinations' rate limit (1 req/15s anonymously), and validates the response
isn't an error page masquerading as an image:

```bash
python "<skill_dir>/scripts/generate_texture.py" "camo military texture, seamless tileable texture, flat lighting, no watermark, high detail" ./textures/gun_camo.png --width 1024 --height 1024
```

Save into a scratch/textures folder, not directly into the user's project tree, unless
they've told you where assets belong. Pick a filename that says what it is
(`gun_gold_plated.png`, not `output.png`) — you'll likely generate a few variants before
landing on one the user likes.

**Show the generated image to the user before uploading it to Roblox.** Generation is
fast and free; asset upload and moderation are not instant, and re-uploading a rejected
or disliked texture wastes a Studio round trip. Get a thumbs-up first unless the user
explicitly says to skip preview and just apply it.

### 3. Upload as an image asset

`upload_image` takes image URLs, not file paths, so serve the textures folder on
localhost for the upload, then stop the server:

```bash
python -m http.server 8765 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory ./textures
```

```
upload_image(imagePaths=["http://localhost:8765/gun_camo.png"], studio_id=...)
```

It returns a map of URL to `rbxassetid://<id>`. (No Studio? The `ul-3d-model`
skill's `upload_asset.py` uploads an Image through Open Cloud with your own
`ROBLOX_API_KEY`.) **Uploads go through asset moderation** and can take a while
before they render; a freshly uploaded image sometimes shows grey even though the
property is set correctly. If `screen_capture` shows a grey or missing texture right
after upload, that's the likely cause; tell the user rather than assuming the
pipeline failed.

### 4. Apply it to the target

For a single part with a `Texture`/`Decal` child, or a `MeshPart` with a texture
property:

```lua
workspace:FindFirstChild("<target>", true).TextureID = "rbxassetid://<id>"
```

For a `Model` with multiple textured parts (e.g. a gun made of several `MeshPart`s that
should all share the skin), loop over descendants in one `execute_luau` call:

```lua
local model = game.Workspace:FindFirstChild("GunModel", true)
for _, part in ipairs(model:GetDescendants()) do
    if part:IsA("MeshPart") then
        part.TextureID = "rbxassetid://<id>"
    end
end
```

Use `inspect_instance` first if you're not sure whether the target exposes
`TextureID`, `Texture`, or a `SurfaceAppearance` child (SurfaceAppearance/MeshParts with
PBR materials are wired differently than a plain decal) — setting the wrong property
silently does nothing, so it's worth the extra read.

### 5. Verify

Call `screen_capture` and look at the result before telling the user it's done. A
property write succeeding doesn't mean the texture rendered correctly — mismatched UV
mapping, moderation delay, or the wrong property target can all leave the mesh looking
unchanged or wrong even though every tool call returned success.

## Iterating on style

If the user wants variations ("try it more worn", "less shiny"), regenerate with a
tweaked prompt rather than trying to edit the existing image — Pollinations has no
edit/inpaint endpoint in this flow, only text-to-image. Keep the `--seed` fixed across
variants of the *same* concept if you want family resemblance between attempts, and drop
it (or change it) for a genuinely different direction.

## What this skill does not do

- It doesn't replace Roblox's own mesh-aware texturing (the MCP's `generate_texture`,
  or the Texture Generator in Studio), which produces better UV-fitted results on
  complex meshes because it reasons about the geometry. This pipeline's advantage is
  that it's scriptable, tileable and batchable, not that it's higher quality.
- It doesn't manage Roblox asset moderation — uploads can be rejected (e.g. for content
  policy) and that's outside this skill's control. If `upload_image` reports a rejection,
  relay it to the user rather than retrying blindly.

ul-ui-builder.text:
---
name: ul-ui-builder
description: Build Roblox game UI headlessly - HUD overlays, shops, inventories, quest lists, settings - from a JSON spec, and generate the icon set that goes in it. Emits a PNG mockup, a Rojo .model.json and a Luau builder from ONE resolved tree, so the preview cannot drift from what ships. Use whenever the user wants a Roblox GUI, menu, shop UI, HUD, inventory screen or UI mockup made rather than clicked together in Studio, wants game icons generated, wants a UI built from a theme file, or asks why their UI looks flat, breaks on mobile, or renders differently in Studio than in the design.
---

# Roblox UI, headless

> **First time on this machine?** Read `LOCAL.md` in this folder. If it does not exist, run the
> `ul-setup-check` skill (or copy `LOCAL.template.md` to `LOCAL.md` and fill it in).
> `LOCAL.md` holds your paths and tool locations; it is yours and is never shared.

## Quick start: your first HUD in one minute

`examples/coin_hud.json` is a complete, passing spec (a coin counter, top-left).
Copy it next to your game, change it, and build:

```bash
python scripts/ui_build.py examples/coin_hud.json --out build    # PNG + .model.json + Luau
python scripts/verify_ui.py examples/coin_hud.json               # layout, text fit, touch sizes
```

- `"theme": "default"` uses `references/theme.json`. To restyle, copy that file
  next to your spec, edit it, and set `"theme": "mytheme.json"` (see Themes below).
- A label your code fills in at runtime ships as `"<unbound>"` and lists its
  longest real values in `"samples"`, which is what the text-fit check measures.
- Icons need an icons folder passed with `--icons`; leave them out until you have one.

Two halves that meet in the middle: **procedural structure** (about 80% of what
reads as modern Roblox UI needs no image at all) and a **generated icon set** for
the part that does.

Design numbers live in `references/ui-recipes.md`, measured from Roblox staff
posts and four community guides. Read it before inventing a value.

---

## The one idea this skill is built on

**A mockup drawn in a design tool is a picture of a UI, and it drifts.** So there
is no design tool here. One JSON spec resolves to one tree, and that tree emits:

| Output | What it is for |
|---|---|
| `Page.png` | The fast local probe. Sub-second, no Studio, no plugin. |
| `Page.model.json` | The deliverable. Drops into a Rojo project. |
| `Page.lua` | The transport. Paste into `execute_luau`, no Rojo session needed. |

The PNG cannot disagree with the `.model.json` about a size, a colour or a
layout, because neither is authored: both are rendered from the same resolved
tree. The Studio screenshot stays ground truth for what the renderer
approximates (font metrics, gradient banding).

This is the UI stage's version of the 2D concept gate in `ul-3d-model`: put
the checkpoint where judging is cheap and reliable. UI is the only stage that is
natively 2D, so what you screenshot is what ships.

---

## A PLACEHOLDER MUST BE A STRING THE LIVE CODE CAN NEVER PRODUCE

**Never use `--`, `0`, `...`, `—` or an empty string as a dynamic label's
placeholder. Use a sentinel like `<unbound>`.** And then gate on it: every label
carrying the sentinel must be named by some controller, or the build fails.

Measured in a real build. A shipped HUD had four labels - an ammo counter and three
rows of a freezing panel - that **no line of code anywhere could write**. The
ammo count lived in a server-side table that was never broadcast; the freezing
rows were fed from a roster that did not carry a frozen flag. They rendered `--`
for entire runs, in front of the user, while sheep actually froze to death.

Nothing caught it, and the reason is the interesting part:

- `verify_ui.py` passed, because it checks **layout** - nothing touching, nothing
  off-centre, no box round a button. A dead label is laid out perfectly.
- The PNG mockup agreed with the game, because **both are drawn from the same
  tree**. That agreement is this skill's core strength and it is exactly why it
  cannot see this class of bug.
- `--` **reads as a plausible empty value.** It looks like "no ammo yet", not
  like "this label is wired to nothing". A sentinel that no formatter could ever
  emit turns a silent defect into an obvious one on the first screenshot.

The gate is about twenty lines: walk the built `.model.json`, collect every named
node whose `Text` is the sentinel, and require the name to appear in the client
source. Two shapes count as a reference - the literal (`"AmmoCount"`) and an
**assembled** one (`` `BankRow{i}` .. "Name" ``), so split the name on digit runs
and require each segment; a name with no digits must appear literally. Getting
that wrong matters: a first version understood only the literal form and reported
ten *working* labels as dead. **A gate that cries wolf gets switched off, which
is worse than not having one** - so when a new check disagrees with something you
have seen working in game, the check is wrong until proven otherwise.

Then prove the gate fails. Rename one binding, watch it go red, put it back. A
check that cannot fail is not a check.

## Read this first: seven things that will bite

**1. CLIP takes 77 tokens and truncates the rest SILENTLY.** The first icon batch
sent 161. Every isolation clause - "single object", "plain grey background", "no
text" - was cut before the model saw it, and four prompts came back as scenes and
pattern wallpaper. One warning line in a log was the only sign. `kaggle_run.py` (in `ul-3d-model`)
now refuses to push an over-budget prompt, and the framing that decides usability
goes in the prompt HEAD, ahead of the subject.

**2. The Kaggle client RETURNS errors, it does not raise them.**
`dataset_create_new` on an existing dataset returns `status="error"` and the old
code caught only exceptions, so the fallback to `dataset_create_version` never
ran and the dataset sat on version 1 forever. Every reroll silently regenerated
the FIRST batch's prompts, on time, looking plausible. Prompts now carry a
`batch_id`, the kernel echoes it, and `fetch` refuses a mismatch.

**3. `ClipsDescendants` does not clip ROTATED descendants.** The angled chevron
header in every second Roblox UI reference is this trap. It lints clean, exits 0,
and throws diagonal bands across the viewport. Use a `UIGradient` hard
transparency step instead. Construction: draw the
angle as a gradient on the unrotated element, never as a rotated child inside a
clipping parent.

**4. Do not chroma key a generated icon.** Keyers compare Cb/Cr and magenta
shares the Cr axis with red, so a magenta key eats the reds and pinks that fill
an icon set. Generate on flat grey and flood fill from the border instead: this
style has a thick opaque outline, so the fill stops dead at the artwork.
`icon_cutout.py` does it.

**5. A dark stroke of 4 is a HEADING value.** Applied to 24px brown body text on
a cream panel it reads as mud. `textStroke` is explicit per label, and 0 is the
right answer for small dark text.

**6. THE PNG AND THE .model.json CAN AGREE ON EVERY VALUE AND STILL DISAGREE ON
ARRANGEMENT.** This is the one real limit of the "same tree" guarantee, and every
instance of it was found by a Studio render, never by the preview:

- Shadow and Face as SIBLINGS meant a `UIListLayout` gave each shadow its own
  cell - four tabs rendered as eight. Each element is now wrapped so the wrapper
  is the single layout item.
- The decorative `Highlight` frame inside a laid-out face claimed a slot and
  shoved price text out of its button. `UICorner`/`UIGradient`/`UIStroke` are not
  `GuiObject`s so layouts ignore them; only a Frame is caught.
- No `LayoutOrder` meant a grid came back in arbitrary order.
- `TextScaled` fills the whole label box while the renderer uses
  `height * textScale`, so Studio text ran large until a `UITextSizeConstraint`
  capped it.

- `TextScaled` **does not overflow, it SHRINKS** - without limit. So the symptom
  of text that does not fit is never text outside a frame, it is text that has
  quietly become unreadable. The renderer now shrinks to fit exactly as Roblox
  does, and `verify_ui`'s `text_fit` check measures how far each label had to
  shrink and fails below 55% of its designed size or 11pt on the worst device.
  It caught three on the first run, all descriptive text sized for a monitor.

**Render one page in Studio before trusting a set of them.**

**7. Never replace a directory inside a cloud-synced folder.**
`mv` plus `cp -r` made the sync client write conflict copies named
`<file>-<machine name>.png` holding the NEW images while the OLD files kept the
canonical names. 37 icons updated, 4
silently did not, and it surfaced only as two stale icons in a screenshot. Copy
file by file.

---

## Workflow

### 1. Icons

Every icon in this skill is generated or drawn by the skill itself (no third-party icon pack is needed). A page builds before any icon exists: an `icon` element with no matching PNG is skipped in the preview and carries a named placeholder in the emitted tree.

**Generate on Cloudflare, not on a GPU.** Measured on the same prompts:

| | Kaggle / SDXL | Cloudflare / FLUX.1-schnell |
|---|---|---|
| Per icon | 59s | **1.2s** |
| 33-icon set | ~40 min | **~40s** |
| Rejected by the checks | 12 of 38 | **0 of 33** |

The reason is hardware, not prompting. Kaggle hands out a Tesla P100 (sm_60,
2016) or a T4, with no way to choose, and **neither supports bf16** - which every
current model is built around. A 12B FLUX-class model dies with CUDA OOM on that
card even with CPU offload. Cloudflare runs it on their hardware and returns a
PNG.

    python scripts/gen_icons_cf.py --manifest <your icons manifest>.json         --out <project>/_cf_raw
    python scripts/icon_cutout.py --in <project>/_cf_raw --out <project>/icons         --size 256 --sheet <project>/icons_sheet.png
    python scripts/glyphs.py --out <project>/icons --size 256
    python scripts/upload_icons.py --icons <project>/icons --map <project>/icons.json

`references/icons.example.json` shows the manifest format (a shared `style`
anchor plus one short subject prompt per icon). Needs `CF_ACCOUNT_ID` and
`CF_API_TOKEN` (Account > Workers AI > Read). The
budget is **10,000 neurons/day**, and the MEASURED cost is **~141 neurons per
1024px 4-step image**, so about **70 images/day**. The published per-tile formula
predicts 57.6 and is 2.4x optimistic - trust the dashboard, not the price list.

Two operational facts: the endpoint takes **only `prompt` and `steps`** (width,
height and seed return HTTP 400, so there is **no seed** and a reroll is a real
reroll), and the safety filter throws false positives - "one metal grain silo
tower" came back NSFW, which needs a **reword, not a retry**.

Then **look at the sheet**. The check that matters is `extra_objects`: image
models pluralise small nouns, and a sheet of seven chickens passes every colour
statistic ever written. A multi-object generation is CROPPED to the best object
plus anything clustered with it, and flagged `SALVAGED` so it gets looked at.

**SYMBOLS ARE DRAWN, NOT GENERATED**, and that held for every model tried.
`glyphs.py` draws close, tick, heart, star, lock, plus, minus and arrow with a
dilation-based uniform outline. Generated attempts returned a scribble for the X,
a down-arrow for the tick and a games controller for the heart. Geometry is not
an image-generation problem, and a drawn set is consistent by construction.

Kaggle stays the right venue for the 3D mesh stage, where a long GPU session with
a big repo suits a notebook. If you use it, `PYTHONUTF8=1` on `fetch` is not
optional on Windows - the Kaggle client writes the log with the default codec and
dies on cp1252 partway through.

### 2. Pages

Write a small spec generator (a Python script that builds the dicts with
`scripts/ui_kit.py`), not five hand-edited JSON files. A typical set is five
pages: HUD, shop, inventory, quests, settings.

```bash
python scripts/ui_build.py <your spec>.json --out mockups --icons icons
# builds all three outputs; pass --png / --model / --luau to build only some
```

Elements: `panel`, `button`, `frame`, `label`, `icon`. Containers take
`layout: {type: list|grid, ...}`, `padding` and `aspect`. Sizes and positions are
UDim2 `[sx, ox, sy, oy]` with an `anchor` - Roblox's rules, not CSS.

Every `panel` and `button` expands to **the depth stack** automatically: a shadow
offset down in a darker, hue-shifted-toward-blue colour, a face with a top-lit
`UIGradient` at rotation -90, and a dark outer `UIStroke` of identical thickness
everywhere. That stack is the whole difference between flat and professional in
both community guides, and it is not a per-element decision.

The guides' **inset bright highlight is OFF by default**. It reads as a lit
edge on a saturated Figma button and as a second border with a visible gap in
Roblox; on cream panels it looked like white lines drawn on everything. The
gradient already carries the top-light. Re-enable per element with
`highlight: true`, or theme-wide.

### 3. Into Studio

Paste `Page.lua` into `execute_luau`, then `capture_screenshot`. A `ScreenGui`
under `StarterGui` renders live in the viewport, so the UI is checkable in EDIT
mode with no playtest: the viewport renders a `ScreenGui` under `StarterGui` live,
so drive the real controller into it and screenshot. Clear the injected
instances afterwards so the saved place carries no drift.

Icons still need real asset IDs. `to_instances` emits
`rbxassetid://ICON_<NAME>` placeholders - upload with `ul-3d-model`'s
`upload_asset.py` as **assetType Image, never Decal** (a Decal wraps an image and
has a different id; assigning it renders nothing, with no error), then
substitute.

---

### 4. Responsiveness

Pages are authored at a **reference resolution in offset** - which is how the
guides build, and what keeps a design predictable - and mapped to the player's
screen by **one `UIScale` on the CanvasFrame**, fitted by
`references/UIController.client.lua` from the page's `AbsoluteSize` (the full screen area) and refit
whenever that changes. `Camera.ViewportSize` is the device safe area and is not used for the fit.

There is deliberately **no floor** on that scale. A floor of 0.60 was tried and
was the wrong lever: it made the page render at 768x432 on a 640x360 phone, so it
stopped FITTING, which is worse than being small.

Touch targets are protected at the source instead. 44pt on a 640x360 phone means
**88px at a 1280x720 reference**, so `ui_kit.TOUCH_H` is 88 and every interactive
control is sized from it. That is what "mobile first" actually costs, and it is
why the shop TILE is the button rather than a small pill inside it.

`verify_ui.py` evaluates every page at four real viewports (640x360, 896x414,
1024x768, 1920x1080), applies the scale, and fails anything under the minimum
with the exact px it needs. Run it before believing a page works anywhere but
your monitor.

---

## Layout hygiene: the three things a human notices in one second

These are the complaints a player makes about a UI that passed every other check
on this list, and they are now enforced by `verify_ui.py` rather than left to
taste. They are measured on the RESOLVED rectangles at the reference resolution,
not read off the property tree, because every one of them is a rendering fact.

**1. ELEMENTS MUST NEVER TOUCH.** Minimum 8px between siblings at the reference
resolution; an overlap is a failure, a gap under 8px is a warning. Two controls
with no space between them read as one control with a line through it, and at the
smallest supported scale a 1px gap is a 0px gap. Anything meant to sit on top of
something else - a sweep over a cooldown dial, a value over a bar - declares
itself with `"overhang": true`, so that "these overlap" always means either a bug
or a decision somebody wrote down. Checks: `sibling_overlap`, `sibling_gap`.

**2. CENTRED IS A MEASUREMENT, NOT A PROPERTY.** An element that asks to be
centred has its rendered centre compared against its parent's, to 1.5px. The
classic Roblox bug is a `0.5` scale position with no `0.5` anchor: the element
lands **half its own size** off centre, which looks almost right, and it is
exactly the error the checker names when it sees it. Never eyeball centring off a
mockup - the mockup is drawn from the same numbers that are wrong. Check:
`off_centre`.

**3. NO BOX DRAWN AROUND A CONTROL.** A frame that exists only to position
something must be `"transparent": true`. An opaque container hugging one child -
within 6px on every side - is not a container, it is an outline nobody asked for,
and it is the box-around-a-button defect. The same
applies to a bar's track hugging its fill. If a control needs a visible border,
that is a stroke or a padded panel with a stated padding, not an accidental
wrapper. Check: `wrapper_box`.

**A note on what these checks cost.** They fire on layouts that were signed off
by eye and by every other gate, which is the point - but a warning is not a
licence to widen every gap to 8px mechanically. Read what it names, then either
fix the spacing or declare the overlap. What is not acceptable is leaving it
unexamined because the page "looks fine" in the mockup at 1280x720.

## Iterate on `verify_ui.py`, not on the mockup

The mockup PNG is for a human and for sign-off. It is not the iteration loop:
an image is re-sent on every later tool call in the same context, so re-opening
it after each tweak is the most expensive way to ask a question the checker
already answers in text. `verify_ui.py` names the element, the number and the
rule it broke. **Fix against the text, then look at the PNG once, when the page
is done.**

This is not a licence to skip the look. The checker cannot see taste, colour
weight, or whether a screen reads at a glance - and it is drawn from the same
resolved tree as the layout, so it agrees with the layout by construction. One
honest look at the end, at the reference resolution.

## Non-negotiables

- **Scale, not Offset**, for size and position. The exception is
  `UIStroke.Thickness`, which genuinely has no scale.
- **Touch targets 44pt minimum.** Action buttons 70x70 on small screens.
- **Keep the thumbstick zone (bottom left), the jump zone (bottom right) and the
  36px top bar clear.** Put a hotbar bottom-CENTRE for exactly
  this reason.
- **One frame per page**, transparent, so a scripter toggles one `.Visible`.
- **`UIAspectRatioConstraint` inside grid cells**, or tiles distort.
- **Stroke thickness identical across the screen.** Mixed weights is the single
  clearest tell of beginner or generated UI.
- **Text must fit its box at a legible size**, checked by `text_fit`. Do not
  "solve" a long string by shrinking the label; widen the box or shorten the text.
- **Never hardcode a text colour.** Use `ink`, `inkSoft`, `onDark` from the theme.
  A test on a dark theme produced perfect layout with invisible item
  names because one component had a light-panel brown baked in.
- **Green price buttons, with the currency icon on them.** A convention, not a
  preference.
- **Nothing touches, everything that says it is centred is centred, and no frame
  draws a box round its child.** See "Layout hygiene" above - three checks, all
  enforced.

---

## Themes: writing your own theme file

A spec's `"theme"` is either an inline object or a path to a JSON file, resolved
relative to the spec. `references/theme.json` is the default and the template to
copy. Every value in it is read by the renderer and the emitter from the one
file, so changing it restyles the PNG and the `.model.json` together.

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stroke` | Outer `UIStroke` thickness on panels and buttons (default theme: 5) |
| `textStroke` | Default text stroke (4); override per label, 0 for small dark text |
| `corner` | Corner radius as a scale (0.2) |
| `shadowOffset` | Pixels the depth-stack shadow sits below the face (7) |
| `outline` | Hex colour of every stroke |
| `backdrop` | Preview-only ground: one hex, or two hexes for a vertical gradient |
| `backdropImage` | Optional preview-only screenshot of your game world to judge the UI over; never emitted |
| `palette` | Named colours (`panel`, `gold`, `green`, `ink`, `onDark`, ...). Elements refer to them by name; never hardcode a text colour |
| `font`, `fontStyle` | `FredokaOne` (default, bundled), `BuilderSans`, `SourceSans`, `Merriweather`, `Montserrat`. Only Fredoka previews exactly; the others fall back to a system font in the PNG and Studio is truth |
| `flat` | `true` emits solid fills instead of the top-lit gradient |
| `highlight` | `true` turns the inset highlight on theme-wide |
| `motion` | Hover, press and open-style numbers, emitted as attributes and played by `references/UIController.client.lua` |

Panels take `alpha` for translucency.

**Surfaces carry a PATTERN layer, not just a gradient.** `scripts/patterns.py` draws
sheen, stripes, dots, clouds and grain; any panel/button/frame takes
`"pattern": {name, colour, opacity, tile, fade}`. Leaving it out is why a UI built
from shapes alone reads flat. Upload `pattern_*.png` with the icons. A patterned
surface moves its children into a `Content` frame so a layout never grabs the
pattern.

**Motion is data too.** A theme's `"motion"` block (hover scale/rotate/time/style,
press scale/time, page open style) is emitted as attributes and played by
`references/UIController.client.lua`. Many games open menus INSTANTLY and put the
motion on buttons and content. The PNG cannot prove motion - playtest it.

## References

- `references/ui-recipes.md` - the measured numbers, the depth stack, page
  composition, and the sources
- `references/icons.example.json` - an example icon manifest showing the prompt
  budget and the shared style anchor
- `references/theme.json` - the default theme, the template for your own
- `references/fonts/` - Fredoka and Fredoka One, used by the renderer. These font
  files are licensed under the SIL Open Font License (OFL) and may be redistributed.

## Gamepad and keyboard focus

Every page's CanvasFrame sets `SelectionGroup = true`, so gamepad focus cannot leave an open page
for a control behind it. When a page opens on a gamepad, the controller calls `GuiService:Select` on
the page, which picks the selectable control with the smallest `SelectionOrder`. Escape and the
gamepad B button close the top page. Give the control you want focused first a lower
`SelectionOrder`. Gamepad input is not testable from the Studio tools; it is UNVERIFIED until a
person plays it.

## Runtime modules (references/)

- `UIFormat.luau` - `compact` (1.2K, 3.4M) and `clock` (m:ss.cc, h:mm:ss). Pure functions, tested in Studio.
- `UIBind.luau` - binds a label to an attribute. A missing value shows `<unbound>`, the same sentinel
  `verify_labels.py` checks, so a binding and the gate agree.
- `UIToast.luau` - a queue of short messages, one at a time, below the top bar.

## `scripts/check_contrast.py` - the colour contrast gate

```bash
python scripts/check_contrast.py references/theme.json
```

Checks the text colours a theme declares against the surfaces they sit on (WCAG contrast, 4.5:1).
It measures flat fills only: a stroke or a gradient does not count, so a failing pair can still read
in the game, and a passing pair is only a floor. See `references/ui-roadmap.md` for what it found.

## `verify_labels.py` - the dead-label gate

```bash
python verify_labels.py --ui src/ui --client src/client
```

Every label carrying the placeholder sentinel must be named by some controller,
or the build fails. This is the gate for the placeholder rule at the top of this
file, and it is proven to fail: rename one binding and it goes red.

It understands two shapes of reference - the literal (`"AmmoCount"`) and one
ASSEMBLED from a row index (`` `BankRow{i}` .. "Name" ``), because a first
version understood only the literal and reported ten WORKING labels as dead.
`--sentinel` overrides the default `<unbound>`; whatever you choose, it must be a
string the live code can never produce.

## Icon bank and name contract

- `scripts/gen_icon_bank.py`: turns `icons.json` (from the icon upload step) into a Luau icon bank module. `ui_build.py` strips Image properties, so icons are loaded from this bank at runtime.
- `scripts/verify_name_contract.py`: checks that the shipped screens contain every name the client code binds to, using `ui/name_contract.json`. Use it when controllers were written before the real UI.

## Check-Clean-UI style (check-ui-rules): mandatory for every GUI feature

Before you build any screen, read `skills/check-ui-rules/SKILL.md` (Check-Clean-UI). It sets the cartoon style: GothamBlack text with outlines, slate-blue windows, 38x38 close buttons, the two-tier header divider, the checkerboard texture, and camera-based scaling.

- It is required for every GUI feature. Do not mix it with a theme file's colours and fonts on the same screen.
- Its texture asset ID (`rbxassetid://385956923`) is UNVERIFIED. Confirm the asset loads and check its licence before a screen uses it. Never copy an ID you have not confirmed.

ul-vfx-library.text:
---
name: ul-vfx-library
description: Harvest free Creator Store VFX packs, which you have taken into your own Roblox account, into your own searchable library of portable JSON particle recipes by reading every emitter property out of Studio, then classify, find, curate and emit them as a Luau runtime module (VFXKit) that builds them on any part with scale and tint. No effects ship with this skill, only the tooling. Verified by phase-frozen edit-mode screenshots, never by a metric. Use whenever the user wants a Roblox particle effect, explosion, aura, hit effect, fire, smoke, sparks or magic effect found and wired rather than dragged in by hand, wants to build a reusable VFX library from packs they own, or asks why their ParticleEmitter is invisible, never stops, or looks nothing like it did in the pack they copied it from.
---

# Roblox VFX, headless

A VFX effect is not an asset. It is about thirty numbers per layer plus a texture
reference. That single fact decides this skill's whole architecture: recipes are
**portable JSON you own**, and the only part you do not own is the texture.

---

## Start here (cold session)

> **First time on this machine?** Read `LOCAL.md` in this folder. If it does not exist, run the
> `ul-setup-check` skill (or copy `LOCAL.template.md` to `LOCAL.md` and fill it in).
> `LOCAL.md` holds your paths and tool locations; it is yours and is never shared.

**This skill is a harvester, not a pack.** It ships tooling and no effects. You
build your own library, in this order:

1. **Take free VFX packs into your own Roblox account, by hand.** Find a pack on
   the Creator Store (or in Studio's Toolbox) and press its Get / Add to
   Inventory button while signed in. This step cannot be automated: `insert_asset`
   and `InsertService:LoadAsset` both refuse an asset your account does not own,
   with "User is not authorized to access Asset", **even when the listing says
   free**. Free means free to take, not free to load. (Roblox's own "Particle
   Effects" pack, `228304820`, is the one exception measured: it loads without
   being taken, which makes it the test pack.)
2. **Put the pack in a Studio place** (drag it from your inventory into
   Workspace, in any place you have open).
3. **Run the harvester** (`payload.py harvest` + `recipe_server.py`, below). The
   recipes land in YOUR library folder, outside the skill folder. The path is in
   `LOCAL.md` (`ROBLOX_VFX_LIB`).
4. **Classify, find, curate, emit** from your own library: `classify_lib.py`
   tags it, `find_vfx.py` searches it, `audition.py` compares candidates,
   `curate.py` copies the ones a game uses, `emit_luau.py` writes the
   `VFXKit` ModuleScript.

Keep your library private. Using a free pack's assets in your own game is within
the Creator Store terms; extracting their values and textures and redistributing
them as your own pack is a different act.

**Layout.** The skill and a library are separate on purpose: a library holds
extracted packs, so it lives OUTSIDE the skill directory and every script takes
`--lib` (or reads the `ROBLOX_VFX_LIB` environment variable).

```
<skill>/
  SKILL.md          this file
  LOCAL.md          your machine-specific settings (from LOCAL.template.md)
  scripts/          the tooling (below)
  scripts/luau/     codec + harvest + build bodies, assembled by payload.py
  references/       VFXKit.lua (an empty generated kit) + a worked runtime script
  work/             scratch payloads, also served over localhost

<your library folder>/     path set in LOCAL.md, outside the skill folder
  harvested/        raw intake from the harvester. Look at it, then promote.
  recipes/*.json    the recipes you kept
  compositions/     optional: timelines you author over your recipes
  index.json        search index, built by classify_lib.py
  .cache/           texture thumbnails + tag caches, all regenerable
```

**Entry points**, all `--lib`-aware:

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `find_vfx.py --lib DIR <words> --layered` | find effects by what they ARE |
| `payload.py build --recipe F --target PATH --out work/b.lua` | assemble a build payload |
| `recipe_server.py` | sink for harvests **and** serves `work/*.lua` over localhost |
| `verify_vfx.py --lib DIR --quiet` | defect checks; `--self-test` proves they can fail |
| `classify_lib.py --lib DIR` | (re)build `index.json`; `--sheet ring` audits labels |
| `payload.py harvest --root PATH --out work/h.lua` | harvest a pack out of Studio |

**Before touching Studio**, confirm your Studio bridge is actually live. A
connected plugin and a working one are different things. With Roblox's official
Studio MCP (recommended), run a trivial `execute_luau` (`return 1`) and take a
`screen_capture`; where this file says `capture_screenshot`, that is the official
server's `screen_capture`. With the older third-party `robloxstudio-mcp` server:

```bash
curl -s localhost:48741/health
```

`"pluginConnected": true` is the only signal that means anything there. If that
looks fine and tools still time out, see *"When the MCP is connected but every call
times out"* below.

**To build and judge effects from a library**, go to *"Previewing a harvested
recipe"*. To add packs to one, go to *"Harvesting a pack"*.

---

## The one idea this skill is built on

**Do not generate particle parameters. Retrieve them.**

Generating a good emitter from a text prompt is unverifiable offline, because
nothing outside Roblox simulates a ParticleEmitter. Retrieving an effect a human
artist already tuned is trivially verifiable and immediately correct. This is the
same T1/T2 logic that makes Creator Store audio the right answer over generated
SFX.

What makes it a skill rather than copy-paste is the layer on top:

```
free VFX pack in Studio
   -> harvest.lua (explicit property walk)  -> recipe JSON (yours, portable)
   -> tune live in Studio, harvest back     -> recipe JSON (updated)
   -> emit_luau.py                          -> VFXKit ModuleScript
   -> VFXKit.build(name, part, {scale, tint, lifetime_mul, rate_mul, offset})
```

Retrieval gives you an explosion. The transform layer gives you "that explosion,
0.6 scale, tinted green, fired at this attachment on this event".

**This skill is the harvester, not the harvest.** Using free pack assets in your
own game is within the Creator Store terms. Extracting their values and
redistributing them as your own pack is a different act, and the textures are
unambiguously someone else's work. So the skill contains the tooling and each
user builds their own library from packs in their own account.

---

## Read this first: fifteen things that will bite

**1. The MCP's generic property reader sees 18% of a ParticleEmitter.**
`get_instance_properties` and `get_class_info` both return the same nine-field
generic view: `Size`, `Rotation`, `Transparency`, `Color`, `Enabled`,
`Brightness`, Name/ClassName/Parent. **Missing: `Rate`, `Lifetime`, `Speed`,
`SpreadAngle`, `Drag`, `Acceleration`, `Texture`, `LightEmission`,
`EmissionDirection`, `Shape`, `ZOffset`, `Squash`, `FlipbookMode`,
`LockedToPart`** and more. Measured: 6 of 31 real properties. Harvest through
those tools and every recipe looks populated and is three quarters empty,
silently. **Always harvest with `execute_luau` and an explicit property walk**
(`scripts/luau/harvest.lua`). `verify_vfx.py` fails a recipe with a short
property set for exactly this reason.

**2. FIVE stock particle textures exist, and one obvious-looking path is a
trap.** This said "only three" until a real pack was harvested. The first pass
only probed `textures/particles/*.dds` and never looked in `textures/` itself,
so two live paths were being hard-failed as nonexistent. Measured by rendering
each one:

| Path | Looks like | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| `textures/particles/sparkles_main.dds` | soft 8-point star | embers, motes, magic |
| `textures/particles/fire_main.dds` | noisy orange flame | fire bodies, explosions |
| `textures/particles/smoke_main.dds` | soft round puff | smoke, dust, glow cores, auras |
| `textures/explosion.png` | puffy lit explosion cloud | blasts, impacts, cartoon fire |
| `textures/sparkle.png` | hard 8-point star, dark rim | sharp sparks, hit flashes |

**`rbxasset://textures/smoke.png` renders NOTHING** — and Roblox's own
"Particle Effects" pack (`228304820`) ships a Smoke layer pointing straight at
it. A first-party pack contains a permanently invisible emitter. So do
`textures/fire.png` and `textures/particle.png`. Everything under
`textures/particles/` other than the three above (`explosion01_*`,
`light_diffuse`, `smoke_dust`, `burst`, `slash`, `glow`, `star`,
`sparkles_bright`) is also dead.

A wrong texture path is an invisible emitter, not an exception. `verify_vfx.py`
names the three measured-dead paths explicitly rather than reporting them as
generic unknowns, because "not in the stock set" reads like a false positive
when the path came out of a Roblox pack.

**3. An Attachment under a Model or Folder has no world position.** Build targets
must be a `BasePart`. Parent an Attachment anywhere else and the emitters build
silently at the world origin: the effect "works", it is just nowhere near the
thing it belongs to. `VFXKit.build` asserts on this.

**4. A Sphere-shaped emitter on an Attachment spawns from a near-unit volume.**
There is no emitter-size property. On a character that means every particle is
born *inside* the torso and is occluded by it. To surround a character the
particles must either be big enough to overlap the silhouette or be given enough
outward speed to escape it. Use both for an aura.

**5. `capture_screenshot` needs the Studio window FOREGROUNDED, not merely
un-minimised.** A minimised window fails with *"Ensure the Studio viewport is
visible... Known Roblox bug: capture may fail if viewport renders a solid
color."* The message blames the viewport colour. It cost three wrong hypotheses
(backdrop size, `TimeScale`, an over-bright PointLight) before checking
`IsIconic`.

`IsIconic == false` is **not sufficient** — a restored-but-background window
still times out. What reliably works is maximise plus foreground:

```powershell
[W]::ShowWindow($h, 3)          # SW_MAXIMIZE
[W]::SetForegroundWindow($h)
```

The solid-colour failure is real too, so keep some sky or ground in frame rather
than filling it with one flat backdrop.

**6. `execute_luau` silently drops EVERY print if the script yields at all.**
Not just prints after a trailing wait: a script whose *first* statement is a
yielding call (`InsertService:LoadAsset`, `GetKeyframeSequenceAsync`) returns
`success: true` with an EMPTY output array, losing prints that ran long before
the return. "Keep the waits short" does not help when the yield is the work.

The fix is to stop using the return channel for anything that yields: do the
work in `task.spawn`, write progress into a `StringValue`, and read it back in a
**second** `execute_luau` call.

```lua
local sv = Instance.new("StringValue"); sv.Name = "__probe"; sv.Parent = game.ReplicatedStorage
task.spawn(function()
    ...                       -- yields freely
    sv.Value = "DONE :: " .. result
end)
return "spawned"              -- returns immediately, output intact
```

Because it is written on every iteration it also survives a script that dies
half way, which a print does not.

**7. A burst layer with `Rate > 0` bursts AND streams forever.** The commonest
authoring slip, and it reads as "the effect never stops". `VFXKit.build` forces
`Rate = 0` on any layer whose emit mode is `burst`, and the verifier fails it.

**8. Dark smoke on a dark backdrop is invisible, and that is a staging artifact,
not a bug in the effect.** Judge every effect over BOTH a light and a dark
surface before changing a value. A smoke layer was nearly deleted as "not
working" when it was reading perfectly well against the ground.

**9. Real packs parent emitters straight to a Model, where they render
nothing.** Measured on Roblox's own `228304820`: `Model 'Particles'` with three
ParticleEmitters as direct children — no Attachment, no BasePart anywhere. A
ParticleEmitter under a Model has no world position and does not draw at all.
The pack is a *bag of parts* meant to be dragged onto something, not a working
effect. So **an inserted pack looking dead in the viewport tells you nothing
about the recipes inside it**; harvest first and judge after the rebuild.
`harvest.lua` records `parent_class` and `renders_in_place: false`, and the
verifier warns rather than fails, because the values are perfectly good.

**10. Setting `CurrentCamera.CFrame` in edit mode does not stick.** Studio's own
camera controller overwrites it between `execute_luau` calls, so a rig staged at
a fixed world position is often out of frame by the time you capture. Do the
opposite: read `CurrentCamera.CFrame`, then place the rig at
`cf.Position + cf.LookVector * d` and spread it along `cf.RightVector`. Screen
order is then left-to-right in the order you place, which is what makes a
labelled contact sheet trustworthy.

---

**11. `GetFullName()` IS NOT UNIQUE, and using it as a grouping key loses
recipes silently.** Ten sibling Parts all called `Part` under one Folder return
the *same* string. Keying groups on it merges unrelated effects into one giant
recipe AND makes them overwrite each other on write. Measured on a real place:
**366 of 583 recipes vanished**, and what survived included 40- and 55-layer
"effects". Key groups on the **instance itself**, then disambiguate the recorded
path with a `#n` suffix. The sink refuses to overwrite a file whose
`source_path` differs, as a second line of defence.

**12. `PostAsync` refuses a large body, and the fallback print is invisible.** A
1447-recipe pack encodes to ~2MB and the POST throws. The `pcall` catches it,
the code falls back to chunked printing — and if the harvest is running inside
`task.spawn` (which it must be, see trap 6) those prints are dropped too. The
pack reported *"harvested 1447"* and wrote **nothing**. Post in batches of ~40,
and **return the count that reached disk, never the count that was scanned.** A
harvester that reports what it walked rather than what it saved is lying by
construction.

**13. Most pack containers are named `Part`, `Model` or a number.** 61% of
emitters in a real 3100-emitter place. Naming recipes after the nearest
container yields hundreds of files called `Part.json` — complete, verified, and
impossible to search, which is the same as not having harvested it. Climb past
generic names to the nearest ancestor a human actually named, but **never as far
as the harvest root** or the whole pack collapses into one recipe.

**14. Half of what is sold as a "VFX pack" is a TEXTURE LIBRARY.** Shape:
`Part '78'` -> `Attachment` -> `ParticleEmitter 'Images/Lightning'`, one emitter
each, hundreds of them. Single-layer recipes are **correct** here, not a grouping
bug — and the only human-meaningful name is on the **layer**, not the container.
So when the container name is junk and the recipe has one layer, name it from the
layer (`Images/Lightning` -> `Lightning`); when the layer is called `Texture`
too, fall back to the texture asset id, which is at least unique and matches back
to the image. That turned 1660 unfindable files into 1124 human-named ones.


**15. A harvested effect is tuned for the stage it was harvested against, and
`LightEmission = 1` is the trap.** It makes a ParticleEmitter quad ADDITIVE: it
adds to what is behind it instead of covering it. Most packs are shot against a
dark stage, where that reads as glow. Put the same effect over a pale
environment - white stone, snow, an overcast sky - and every quad saturates to
flat white across its whole area the moment it is drawn, because the background
already sits near the top of the range.

Measured in a pale arena map: a finisher hit put **44% of the frame at full
saturation** for a fifth of a second, blanking both fighters at the exact
instant the player needed to see the hit. Two obvious fixes did nothing, and
both were the wrong shape of fix:

| change | frame fully saturated |
|---|---|
| as harvested | 44.1% |
| flash + core quads cut 2.7x | 44.1% |
| spark count 44 -> 24, sizes cut | ~40% |
| pulse lights 9/14 -> 3.0/4.5, ranges halved | 32.5% |
| **`LightEmission` 1 -> 0.35-0.55** | **15.4%** |

Shrinking the quads could not help, because **the saturated area is set by
coverage, not by any single quad's size** - and coverage barely changed.

Two rules fall out of this:

- **Judge a wash by what it is washing.** A floor going evenly white with its
  texture gone is a light or a blend mode. A burst of quads is not even: it has
  edges and spikes. Look at the peak frame at full resolution before changing a
  number, and measure saturation (`fraction of pixels > 250`) rather than
  eyeballing brightness - a pale arena reads as 4% at rest and 44% at peak, and
  the difference between those two is the whole diagnosis.
- **Check the pulse lights against the constant ones in the same file.** One
  build shipped pulse peaks of 9 and 14 alongside constant glows of 2.2 and 3.0. That
  gap was not a decision, it came straight from the harvest. Anything above about
  4 will wash a pale scene on its own.

**16. A harvested LAYER OFFSET can be structure, and the engine scales it.**
Every layer records where its emitter's attachment sat in the pack. For most
packs that is zero or a small tuning nudge; for a BEAM pack it is the far end of
the beam. `Lava-01` layer `#1` (FireSpecs1) sits 6.25 studs out, and
`Lighting-01`'s `Lightning` layer hangs 9.9 up. The engine multiplies layer
offsets by the element's `scale`, so at depth-4 scales the embers of every fire
stream landed **15-27 studs from their own effect** - a detached clump of specks
floating over the caster, which reads as a separate bug and is not.

Two ways out, both used: select a zero-offset twin where the pack has one
(`Lava-01` `#6` is `#1` with offset 0, byte for byte), or set **`centred: true`**
on the recipe element, which builds every layer on its anchor and ignores the
harvested positions. It is opt-in, so existing compositions are unchanged. Worth
writing a small checker that fails on any selected layer more than 0.05 studs off
its anchor, for any composition set that selects layers by hand.

**17. A ring costs `segments` Neon parts, so size its segments by RADIUS.** Rings
are built as a loop of parts, not one mesh. Setting segments by
depth gave a 1.6-stud heal ring the same 66 parts as a 15-stud
shockwave; a regeneration heal that spawned a fresh ring set every beat built
2473 instances for one cast. `24 + 2.4 * radius` (capped at 64) stays smooth at
every size, and a repeating ring should be RE-CUED (show / radius / fade on the
same id) rather than rebuilt - the timeline drops finished tracks, so a later
cue takes over cleanly as long as two uses of one ring do not overlap.

**18. A composition that draws its effect with Parts is not using this skill.**
The engine CAN build Neon rings, part groups and part-segment bolts, and it is
tempting to build the "structure" of an effect (shock rings, pillars, sigils,
bolts, walls) that way and only sprinkle harvested emitters on top. That is
generating, not retrieving. One large effect set did it: 12 of 1813 library
recipes used, 1,696 part-built elements, and all of it was rejected on review. The
rebuild found a harvested effect for every one of those roles once someone
actually looked (flat shockwave textures, magic circles, tornado loops, frost
shells, aura rigs, beam ribbons, toon bolt sprites). Rules that fell out:

- **Survey before you build**: list the library's effects by pack and name
  (index.json is keyed by FILENAME - joining on the display name drops whole
  packs), audition candidates per role side by side, normalised to one size
  (packs are authored from dot-sized to 35 studs), and write the choice down as
  a role map in data.
- **Audit a candidate at SEVERAL phases.** Realistic-Explosion-01 is a white
  flash for three frames and an orange fireball after; judged at 0.3s it went
  into every element's release, and put fireballs over water auras.
- **A harvested floor wave is a FILLED disc**, where a ring was an outline:
  the same radius covers several times the screen. Size them ~1.3r, not 2r.
- **Count, and gate**: harvested elements vs parts per effect; fail the build
  on any visible part that is not an invisible carrier or a copy of the character.

**20. A tint cannot recolour a texture that carries its own colour.** Tint
multiplies the Color property; the texture multiplies after it. WaterBurst's
`ToonLiquidColor` sheet is baked blue, so "gold honey" rendered murky green and
"pink cake" stayed blue, while its grey `ToonLiquidAlpha` twin tinted perfectly.
A layer whose harvested Color is BLACK (Portal-01's `Portal`) cannot be tinted
at all. Measure each kept layer's texture (the `.cache/tex` PNG) before choosing
a tint, and keep only the grey layers of anything you recolour.

**19. A Roblox script Source must be under 200,000 characters.** Assigning a
longer string throws `Unable to assign property Source`. A shipped effect set
with many harvested recipes crosses that fast (54 recipes: 356K). Split data into
child ModuleScripts holding JSON strings and decode them lazily.

### Element kinds (engine.lua)

| kind / field | What |
|---|---|
| `beam` | one harvested **Beam layer** (`recipe`, `layer`) wired between `from`/`to` anchors (+offsets) or moving parts (`parent`/`to_parent`); `width_mul`, `tint`. Before this no harvested Beam could be used at all. |
| Beam layers **inside** a recipe | wired automatically from the `endpoints` offsets the harvester recorded (aura rigs: floor emitter + rising beams). |
| `chain` | one harvested recipe strung at `points` hosts between two anchors, `jitter` - a line drawn by the harvest's own effects (lightning bolts). |
| `centred` | recipe field: build every layer ON its anchor, ignoring harvested layer offsets (trap 16). |
| `rate_mul`, `rate_cap` | stream a harvested effect at a multiple of its OWN pack rate (`harvested_rate` survives a burst harvest), capped. |

## Compositions (optional, you author them)

A recipe is one harvested effect on one part. A **composition** is a timeline over
several of YOUR recipes plus simple geometry, for effects like "orb forms in the
hand, swells, pulses, releases". The skill ships the engine, not any compositions:
you write the JSON yourself, against recipes from your own library.

```jsonc
{
  "name": "my_effect",
  "title": "My Effect",                  // on-screen button label (emit_scenes.py)
  "duration": 3.0,
  "elements": [
    {"id": "core", "kind": "recipe", "recipe": "MyRecipe",   // a file name in your library
     "anchor": "A_Hand", "scale": 0.8, "layers": ["Core", "#3"]},
    {"id": "ring", "kind": "ring", "anchor": "A_Ground", "radius": 2, "segments": 32}
  ],
  "timeline": [
    {"t": 0.0, "id": "core", "act": "enable", "on": true},
    {"t": 1.2, "id": "ring", "act": "radius", "from": 1, "to": 12, "time": 0.6}
  ],
  "camera": {"look": "A_Chest", "offset": [-12, 6, -18], "fov": 50}   // edit mode only
}
```

- **Element kinds:** `recipe`, `beam`, `chain`, `ring`, `part`, `light`, `group`,
  `bolt`, `trail`, `clone`/`model` (see the kinds table below and `engine.lua`).
- **Cue acts:** `emit`, `enable`, `show`, `hide`, `destroy`, `regen`, `warp`,
  `scale`, `radius`, `fade`, `light`, `spin`, `fly`, `spiral`, `burst`,
  `stagger`, `move`. Cues take `t`, `id`, `act`, and `time` / `from` / `to` /
  `style` (an easing name) where they animate.
- **Anchors** are a name (`A_Ground`, `A_Feet`, `A_Waist`, `A_Chest`, `A_Head`,
  `A_Air`, `A_Sky`, `A_Hand`, `A_Far`) or a literal `[x, y, z]`. In play mode a
  literal is character space: x right, y up, -z forward, from the floor point
  under the character. The edit stage (`stage.lua`) builds a dummy and the same
  anchors so what you judge in edit mode is what the runtime builds.
- **Edit-mode loop:** `compose.py my_effect.json --lib <lib> --freeze 0.45 --out
  work/s.lua`, run the payload, screenshot, then repeat at other phases.
  `stage.lua` moves the Baseplate and spawn, so run it only in a scratch place.
  `compose.py my_effect.json --self-test` proves the composition checks can
  fail.
- **Shipping:** `emit_scenes.py --lib <lib> --comps <your compositions folder>
  --out-dir work` writes a `VFXScenes` ModuleScript (compositions plus their
  de-duplicated recipes) and a `VFXDemo` LocalScript with one key and button per
  composition (the first eight get keys 1-8).
- Beware trap 18: a composition that draws its effect with Parts is generating,
  not retrieving. Use the engine's part kinds for glue, and harvested recipes
  for the visible effect.


## Scale: harvest wide, ship narrow

A real harvest is bigger than you expect. One afternoon over 13 free packs
produced **1813 recipes / 2238 layers**, all verified, with one genuine failure.

**Do not emit the whole library.** `emit_luau.py` inlines every recipe into one
ModuleScript; at this size that is a projected **4.7MB** of Luau, which is not a
thing you put in a game. The library is an *archive to search*, and `VFXKit` is
the *subset you chose*. Curate to the handful an effect actually needs, then
emit.

Expect the shape of a big harvest to be: a long tail of single-layer texture
entries, a small band of genuinely layered effects (153 of 1813 here), and a
handful of Beams. The layered ones are where the craft is; the tail is a
lookup table.

## The verify loop

Nothing offline simulates particles, so the gate is Studio itself, in **edit
mode** (no Play required, confirmed working).

**Phase-frozen capture is the technique that makes this practical.** A burst
lasts under a second, so a screenshot is a coin flip. Instead: emit, `task.wait`
the exact age you want to inspect, then set `TimeScale = 0` on every emitter.
The simulation freezes and stays frozen until you set it back to 1, so the
capture lands on the phase you asked for, every time.

```lua
for _, e in ipairs(handle.emitters) do e.TimeScale = 1; e:Clear() end
handle.emit(1.0)
task.wait(0.22)                       -- the phase you want to judge
for _, e in ipairs(handle.emitters) do e.TimeScale = 0 end
-- now capture_screenshot
```

Sample at least an early phase (is the flash reading), a mid phase (is the shape
right) and a late phase (does it have a tail, or does it just stop).

**The contact sheet ranks candidates. Your eye decides.** No metric in
`verify_vfx.py` judges whether an effect looks good, and none can. What it
catches is the class of defect a still cannot show you: truncated property sets,
emitters transparent for their whole life, burst layers that stream, texture
paths that render as nothing, sequences that do not span t=0..1, portability
flags that contradict the texture refs.

On harvested recipes it also raises two **warnings that are a work queue, not
defects**: layers whose emit mode was inferred rather than recorded, and layers
the source pack had parented somewhere they could not render. Both are things
only a human can settle.

```bash
python scripts/verify_vfx.py --lib DIR --quiet     # your harvested library
python scripts/verify_vfx.py work/harvested/SomePack.json   # one file
python scripts/verify_vfx.py --self-test  # prove the checks can fail (10/10, no library needed)
```

## Harvesting a pack

**Status: the harvester has been run end to end on a real third-party pack and
the round trip is lossless.** Measured on Roblox's own "Particle
Effects" (`228304820`): harvest -> JSON -> rebuild, then a property-by-property
diff of the rebuilt emitters against the originals — **84 of 84 values
identical** across all 31 properties x 3 layers, plus a side-by-side
phase-frozen capture that is indistinguishable. The remaining unknown is pack
*shape*, not fidelity.

### Getting the pack in front of you

**`search_assets` is a dead end. Do not spend time on it.** Through an MCP it
typically returns

```
{"errors":[{"code":0,"message":"Scope not authorized."}]}   # HTTP 403
```

against `/toolbox-service/v2/assets:search`, and renaming the API-key variable
buys nothing. A new Open Cloud key with Creator Store scope would be needed.

**You do not need one.** The endpoint Studio's own toolbox uses takes **no auth
at all**:

```bash
curl "https://apis.roblox.com/toolbox-service/v1/marketplace/10?limit=20&keyword=vfx%20pack&sortType=3"
```

```bash
curl "https://apis.roblox.com/toolbox-service/v1/items/details?assetIds=ID1,ID2"
```

`marketplace/10` returns asset IDs (10 = Model) with a `nextPageCursor`;
`items/details` returns name, creator, `createdUtc`, `categoryPath`,
`fiatProduct.isFree` and `capabilities.shouldSandbox`. That is everything
`search_assets` would have given you.

**The real blocker is insertion, not discovery.** `insert_asset` and
`InsertService:LoadAsset` both fail on an unowned Creator Store asset with
**"User is not authorized to access Asset"** — and this is true even when
`isFree: true` and `purchasable: true`. Free does not mean loadable. The asset
has to be **taken into your account first**, through the Creator Store or the
Studio toolbox, by you, by hand. No script can do that step for you.

Measured across 33 free VFX packs: exactly one loaded without being acquired —
`228304820`, the Roblox-owned one, the only result in the whole sweep with
`shouldSandbox: false`. **Sort candidates by `shouldSandbox` and expect
everything `true` to need acquiring.** So the honest first step of a real
harvest is: *take the packs into your account*, then harvest.

### The run

1. **Start the sink.** It is the real output path — chunked printing works for
   three recipes and falls over for two hundred, and a truncated recipe looks
   exactly like a valid one.

   ```bash
   python scripts/recipe_server.py          # lands in <ROBLOX_VFX_LIB>/harvested
   ```

   It lands harvests in `harvested/`, not your curated `recipes/` folder, on
   purpose. A sink pointed at `recipes/` makes thirty unlooked-at recipes
   indistinguishable from the ones you chose. Promote by hand.

2. **Assemble the payload.**

   ```bash
   python scripts/payload.py harvest --root Workspace.SomePack --out work/h.lua
   ```

3. **Run it via `loadstring`, not by pasting.** `loadstring` **is** available in
   plugin context (measured), and the sink serves `work/*.lua` over localhost,
   so payload size stops being a constraint entirely:

   ```lua
   local src = game:GetService("HttpService"):GetAsync("http://127.0.0.1:48752/payload/h.lua")
   local fn, err = loadstring(src)
   if not fn then print("COMPILE_ERROR " .. tostring(err)) return end
   return fn()
   ```

   Expect `HARVEST_POSTED recipes=N len=M`. If the sink is down it falls back to
   chunked printing and says so, so a forgotten sink is a slow path, not a
   silent truncation.

4. **Verify, then curate, then promote.**

   ```bash
   python scripts/verify_vfx.py --lib "<your library>/harvested" --quiet
   ```

5. Move the keepers from `harvested/` into `recipes/`, run
   `classify_lib.py --lib <your library>`, then `emit_luau.py --lib
   <your library>/recipes` (or `curate.py` first, for a game-sized subset).

**Harvest at the container level, never the individual emitter.** A real effect
is three or four layers (a fast bright core, a slower body, high-drag sparks, a
brief light). Index single emitters and you get a bag of parts with no memory of
what they belonged to.

### What the harvester infers, and why you must look

A pack records **no emit metadata**. It ships emitters `Enabled = false` with a
live `Rate`, which means "turn me on for a moment" — a one-shot in everything
but name, with the window nowhere in the data. So `harvest.lua` guesses:
`count = clamp(round(Rate * 0.1), 1, 250)`, and marks the layer
`"inferred": true` with `burst_window` and `harvested_rate` both kept so nothing
is silently lost. The verifier **warns** on every inferred layer.

Treat that warning as the curation queue. On `228304820`, `Rate = 1000` became
`count = 100`; whether the artist meant 40 or 400 is not recoverable from the
asset, only from looking at it.

### Pack shapes that break grouping

`containerOf` walks to the nearest `Model` or `BasePart`. Measured and predicted
failures:

| Pack shape | What goes wrong | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Emitters parented straight to a Model** (MEASURED on `228304820`) | grouping is right, offsets all read `[0,0,0]`, nothing renders in place | correct, not a bug. `parent_class` + `renders_in_place` are recorded; the rebuild puts them on a BasePart and they come back exactly |
| Ten unrelated effects under one Model | all collapse into one giant recipe | group by the nearest ancestor that has a sibling, or split on Attachment when a Part carries several unrelated ones |
| Emitters parented straight to a Part | offsets all read `[0,0,0]` | correct: a Part-parented emitter has no attachment offset |
| Nested Models (effect inside a prop inside a kit) | recipe named after the wrong ancestor | name from the outermost Model whose descendants are ALL vfx classes |

Only the first row has been seen for real. **Do not theorise about which one you
hit. Dump the tree and look** (`get_descendants` with a `classFilter`, or a Luau
walk printing `ClassName/Name/Parent.ClassName`). The input is fully visible.

**Beam and Trail need structure, not values.** `Attachment0`/`Attachment1` are
instance refs, recorded as `{"Ref": "<full name>"}`. Rebuilding means creating
two attachments on the target and pointing the Beam at them, so a Beam recipe
needs an `endpoints` block naming the two offsets. That block does not exist yet
because no Beam has been harvested. Add it when the first one arrives, do not
design it in advance.

**Decide texture provenance at ingest, and expect most packs to fail it.** Good
packs ship their own uploaded textures, so most harvested recipes will come back
`texture_portable: false`. That is fine for use in your own game and it is the
constraint on giving the library away. Sort by it early so the portable ones are
findable. Note that `texture_portable: true` means only *"every ref is an
`rbxasset://` path"* — it does **not** mean the paths resolve. `228304820`
harvested as portable and one of its two textures is dead.

**Curation is the part that is NOT mechanical.** Harvesting thirty recipes
yields thirty recipes, not thirty good ones. Nothing here judges taste. Capture
a preview per recipe, look at them, and delete the dross before indexing.

**If free-pack quality does not clear the bar, the skill does not die.** It
degrades to authoring and applying recipes by hand in the recipe format below.
Harvesting is the accelerator, not the foundation.
