## When the MCP is connected but every call times out

Costs an hour if you have not seen it. `/health` says `pluginConnected: true`
and every tool call returns *"Studio plugin connection timeout"*.

**Applies to the third-party `robloxstudio-mcp` server: two copies are running.** The second one does not enter
proxy mode as intended: `listenWithRetry(app, host, 48741, 5)` succeeds on
**48742**, so it believes it is primary and never promotes. Meanwhile the Studio
plugin only ever polls **48741**. Your tools talk to one server; the plugin
talks to the other, and neither reports anything wrong.

```bash
curl -s localhost:48741/health; curl -s localhost:48742/health
```

Two `"status":"ok"` replies with only one showing `pluginConnected: true` is the
signature. Then:

1. Kill the server holding the port the plugin is on — the one your tools are
   NOT attached to. Killing yours ends the session's MCP.
2. **A raw TCP forwarder from 48741 to your port is enough**, because the plugin
   reconnects to whatever answers on 48741.
3. **The plugin will still show as disconnected.** `GET /poll` does *not*
   register an instance — only `POST /ready` does, and the plugin sends that
   once at startup. Register it yourself, using the `instanceId` its polls
   carry:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:<yourport>/ready \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"instanceId":"<from the /poll query string>","role":"edit"}'
   ```

An ESTABLISHED TCP connection and a 200 on `/poll` both look healthy while the
bridge is doing nothing. `pluginConnected` in `/health` is the only signal that
means anything.

## Previewing a harvested recipe

The loop for judging one recipe out of a library. Everything here is measured;
the traps referenced are the numbered ones above.

1. **Sink up, payload assembled.** The sink also serves payloads over localhost.

   ```bash
   python scripts/recipe_server.py --out "<lib>/harvested"
   ```

   ```bash
   python scripts/payload.py build --recipe "<lib>/recipes/X.json" --target "Workspace.__VFXTarget" --out work/b.lua
   ```

2. **Stage a target RELATIVE TO THE CAMERA.** Setting `CurrentCamera.CFrame` in
   edit mode does not stick (trap 14). Read the camera, then place the part at
   `cf.Position + cf.LookVector * d`. The target must be a `BasePart` (trap 3).
   Put a mid-grey backdrop behind it but keep some sky or ground in frame, or the
   capture fails on the solid-colour bug (trap 5).

3. **Run it via `loadstring`,** not by pasting:

   ```lua
   local fn = loadstring(game:GetService("HttpService"):GetAsync("http://127.0.0.1:48752/payload/b.lua"))
   return fn()
   ```

4. **Emit, then phase-freeze, then capture.** Use the emit count the recipe
   carries, not a number you invented:

   ```lua
   for _, e in ipairs(emitters) do e.TimeScale = 1; e:Clear() end
   for _, e in ipairs(emitters) do e:Emit(e:GetAttribute("EmitCount") or 20) end
   task.wait(0.22)                                   -- the phase you want
   for _, e in ipairs(emitters) do e.TimeScale = 0 end
   ```

   Sample early / mid / late. Maximise and foreground the Studio window first
   (trap 5) — `IsIconic == false` is not enough.

**What you are looking for, beyond "does it look nice":**

- **Is the emit count sane?** Almost every harvested recipe is `emit-inferred`:
  the pack recorded no burst window, so the count is a guess from `Rate * 0.1`
  with `harvested_rate` kept beside it. A faithful recipe with an invented count
  can be five times too dense and still pass every check. **This is the single
  most likely reason a harvested effect looks wrong**, and only your eye finds it.
- **Does it read against BOTH a light and a dark surface?** (trap 8)
- **Does it stop?** A burst layer with `Rate > 0` streams forever (trap 7).

Fix by editing the recipe JSON and rebuilding — the JSON is the source of truth,
and `emit_luau.py` reads the same files, so what you tuned and what ships cannot
disagree.

## Finding anything again: classify, then search

**A harvested library is unusable without this, and that is not a small caveat.**
Names come from whatever the pack author typed. Measured on a real 1813-recipe
library, **only 29% of names say anything at all** — the rest are `Part`, `78`, or
a texture id. The harvest was complete, verified and impossible to search, which
is the same as not having it.

```bash
python scripts/classify_lib.py --lib "~/Roblox-VFX-Library"     # -> index.json
python scripts/find_vfx.py    --lib "~/Roblox-VFX-Library" ice ring --layered
```

Three signals, because no one of them is enough:

| Signal | Coverage | What only it can answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Values** — motion and timing from the harvested props | 100% | one-shot vs continuous, expanding, high-drag, glowing, colour |
| **Sprite** — shape from the texture's pixels | 97% | ring / streak / star / soft — the ONLY signal for texture swatches |
| **Name** — what the artist called it | 29% | `RasenShuriken`. Not derivable from pixels or numbers, and it outranks both |

Together: **98%**.

**Why values alone fail.** A texture-swatch entry is deliberately neutral —
white, speed 0, spread 0, size 1 — so the pack can show off the image. 1552 of
1813 recipes classified identically on values. Everything that distinguishes them
is in the pixels.

**Why the sprite pass needs the flipbook layout.** Most particle textures are
sprite **sheets**, not sprites — 1481 of 2180 layers here are `Grid4x4`. Measure
the whole image and you measure the geometry of the tiling: a 4x4 grid of rings
reads as dense, round and not hollow no matter what the frames hold. Crop to one
frame using the layout the recipe declares, and pick the frame with the most ink,
because frame 0 of a `OneShot` flipbook is usually near-empty.

**Audit the labels before you trust them.**

```bash
python scripts/classify_lib.py --lib DIR --sheet ring
```

That writes a contact sheet with each sprite's assigned tags printed under it.
Look at it. The first version of this classifier scored well and was reading
tiling geometry; the sheet is what showed it. A classifier nobody eyeballed is a
classifier that says yes.

Tags are honest about their own confidence: `is:explosion` came from a name,
`maybe:shockwave` is an inference from sprite shape, and `emit-inferred` means the
burst count was a guess. Search weights them in that order.

## Using it in a game

```lua
local VFXKit = require(game.ReplicatedStorage.VFXKit)

-- "MyAura" and "MyImpact" are recipes in YOUR emitted kit (names you chose in curate.py)
local aura = VFXKit.build("MyAura", character.HumanoidRootPart, {
    tint = Color3.fromRGB(255, 120, 40),   -- keeps the luminance ramp, swaps hue
})
aura.setEnabled(true)

local impact = VFXKit.build("MyImpact", character.HumanoidRootPart, {
    offset = Vector3.new(0, -(humanoid.HipHeight + root.Size.Y * 0.5), 0),
})
impact.emit(1.3)     -- multiplier scales particle counts and light peak
```

`opts`: `scale`, `tint`, `lifetime_mul`, `rate_mul`, `offset`, `suffix`.
`handle`: `emit(mult)`, `setEnabled(bool)`, `destroy()`.

Build twice with the same name and it replaces rather than duplicates. Use
`suffix` for a deliberately independent second instance.

**Tint keeps the luminance ramp and replaces only the hue.** A flat colour swap
destroys the bright-core-to-dark-tail arc, which is the thing that reads as fire.

---

## Recipe format

```jsonc
{
  "name": "MyImpact",
  "duration": 1.9,              // longest tail, for previews
  "texture_portable": true,     // decided at ingest, verified against refs
  "texture_refs": ["rbxasset://textures/particles/fire_main.dds"],
  "layers": [{
    "name": "Fire",
    "class": "ParticleEmitter", // or Beam, Trail, PointLight
    "offset": [0, 0, 0],        // attachment offset from the container origin
    "emit": {"mode": "burst", "count": 16},
    "props": { /* all 31, typed */ }
  }]
}
```

A **harvested** layer carries three extra fields recording where the values came
from. They are provenance, not settings, and hand-authored recipes omit them:

```jsonc
"parent_class": "Model",      // what the emitter hung off in the source pack
"renders_in_place": false,    // ...and whether it could draw there at all
"emit": {
  "mode": "burst", "count": 100,
  "inferred": true,           // NOT recorded by the pack. A guess. Look at it.
  "burst_window": 0.1,        // the guess that produced count
  "harvested_rate": 1000      // the original Rate, which burst mode zeroes
}
```

Typed values, same convention as Rojo `.model.json` so nothing has to be guessed
from a bare array: `{"NumberSequence": [[t, value, envelope], ...]}`,
`{"ColorSequence": [[t, [r, g, b]], ...]}`, `{"NumberRange": [min, max]}`,
`{"Vector3": [x, y, z]}`, `{"Enum": "NormalId.Top"}`.

`emit.mode` is one of `burst` (one-shot `:Emit(count)`), `continuous`
(streams at `Rate`), `pulse` (a light that decays from `from` over `seconds`),
`constant` (a light that stays on).

Beam and Trail `Attachment0`/`Attachment1` are instance references, not values.
They are recorded as `{"Ref": "<full name>"}` and are structure to be rebuilt,
never faked as data.

---

## Performance

- `Rate` is per second and continuous emitters cost every frame. Prefer one-shot
  `:Emit(n)` for anything event-driven.
- Set `LightInfluence = 0` on anything meant to glow, or the world's lighting
  drags it toward grey.
- `LightEmission` is free brightness. A real `PointLight` is not. A typical
  impact recipe uses exactly one, pulsed for about 0.3s.
- Long-lived large soft particles are the expensive case: heavy overdraw. Keep
  aura lifetimes under about a second for this reason.

## Property surface and the self-test

- `references/property-surface.md`: the ParticleEmitter properties that were probed live in Studio (33 candidates, all present). Read it before a recipe sets a property, so the recipe only uses ones that exist.
- `scripts/luau/selftest_client.lua`: a temporary LocalScript for a playtest. It fires every effect in turn and prints what was built to the log, because the MCP cannot read a running game. Remove it after the test.

vfx-and-animation.text:
---
name: vfx-and-animation
description: "any visual effect, particle, trail, beam, highlight, tween, animation, camera shake, screen flash, UI transition or feedback effect."
---

Effects make a game feel good. They are cosmetic and must never decide gameplay.
- Effects are client-side. The server sends the event (what happened, where). Each client draws the
  effect. Do not replicate a particle or tween through a remote every frame.
- Keep effects cheap. Use a small pool of effect Instances, reuse them, and hide or disable them
  instead of creating and destroying them on every hit. Use Debris for one-off effects that must go.
- Limit the count: a fixed maximum number of live effects per type. Drop the oldest, or skip the new.
- Tweens: TweenService:Create(instance, TweenInfo.new(time, Enum.EasingStyle.<style>,
  Enum.EasingDirection.<direction>), goal). Cancel a tween before you start another on the same object.
  Keep most tweens under about one second. Use the same easing for the same kind of motion across the game.
- Animation: load animations through the Animator (an AnimationController's Animator or a Humanoid's
  Animator) with LoadAnimation. Set the track's priority on purpose, and stop tracks you no longer need.
  Check that a custom animation does not override the default walk, run, jump and fall unless that is
  the goal (see roblox-gotchas).
- Particles: use a ParticleEmitter with Emit(count) for bursts. Use Enabled for continuous effects,
  and turn it off when the effect is out of view or the object is hidden.
- Trails and beams: Trail and Beam need two Attachments. Clean them up with the object they follow.
- Highlight outlines: a Highlight can outline a model. Limit how many are on screen at once.
- Camera shake and screen flash: do them on the client only. Keep them short, and restore the camera
  and any overlay state when the effect ends, and on respawn.
- UI feedback: scale or fade a button on press with a short tween, and keep the pressed state visible
  without hover. Respect the reduce-motion idea: keep effects short and avoid strong flashing.
- Check the cost: count the effects and the instances an effect adds, and measure with luau-profiling
  when a change touches a per-frame or per-hit path.
- Verify the APIs for every effect class and enum you use (fetch_roblox_doc), and mark any you could not
  confirm with -- UNVERIFIED: <API name>.
- In the report, say what was checked by reading, and what needs a screen capture or a play test to judge.

agents.agent:ul-agent-animation:
---
name: ul-agent-animation
description: Authors Roblox R15 animations headlessly in Blender from a pose spec and writes a KeyframeSequence spec plus verification renders to disk. Never touches Roblox Studio. Use when the build orchestrator fans out the asset block and needs animation produced in parallel.
maxTurns: 45
skills:
  - ul-animation
effort: medium
color: yellow
---

You produce animation data and the renders that prove it. You have no Studio
tools; the assembly thread registers the KeyframeSequence.

Follow the `ul-animation` skill. Three things from it are load-bearing and
easy to lose under time pressure:

**Animate in FK, not IK.** A KeyframeSequence is per-joint rotations. IK targets
leave limb roll free, so blocky parts flip faces between frames and the colours
pop. Inert bones mean an IK/FK switch, not a dead rig.

**Judge the result by looking at it.** This skill's own tooling has previously
reported success on output that was visibly broken, and its first real test found
five bugs that each made a tool vouch for bad output. When a verifier and the
image disagree, the image wins and the verifier is the thing to audit.

**Probe rather than render to answer a question.** Loading the rig takes under a
second and reading the control map is nearly free, so build the cheap feedback
loop first and produce the expensive render once, at the end.

Report back: the spec path, the contact sheet or GIF path, the rig type (R15
unless briefed otherwise), and your own honest read of whether it looks right. If
it does not, say so rather than passing it on. The assembly thread cannot see your
renders and will take your word for it.
agents.agent:ul-agent-map:
---
name: ul-agent-map
description: Builds a Roblox level from a map spec headlessly - greybox geometry, terrain and the reachability prover - and writes the build artifacts to disk. Never touches Roblox Studio. Use when the build orchestrator fans out the asset block and needs the map produced in parallel with the other asset stages.
maxTurns: 60
skills:
  - ul-map-builder
effort: medium
color: green
---

You produce a map: geometry, terrain, and the report that proves it is playable.
You do not put it into Studio and you have no Studio tools, because the DataModel
is single shared mutable state and exactly one thread may write to it. Your output
is a work folder (default `work/<map name>/`) holding `report.json`, `plan.png`,
`terrain/` for a terrain map, and `build.lua` or `map.rbxmx` from `emit.py`, plus
the spec itself. `skills/ul-map-builder/scripts/build_map.py <spec> --out <folder>` runs prove, plan and
terrain in order and stops on a FAIL.

Follow the `ul-map-builder` skill. Two of its rules are enforced in code, and both
exist because a map passed every check while looking bad:

**GROUND IS TERRAIN.** `spec.py` refuses a spec whose ground is a big flat Part
slab. Declare a `terrain` block, or set `ground_is_parts` with a reason when a
part deck really is the design (a sky arena). Never pass the gate by silence.

**MESH FIRST.** Organic, curved or repeated things (trees, rocks, houses, stalls)
are meshes, not stacks of parts. Use the project's own models or the
ul-3d-model skill, and place them as parts carrying a `mesh` name. Build from a
downloaded reference, never from imagination: one reference produced six concrete
corrections in a single look where reasoning produced a box with a lid three times.

Two traps that exit cleanly while producing a broken map: `volume.lift` has been
dropped by an emitter before, leaving surfaces at exactly y=0.00, so check the
emitted heights rather than the spec's; and a boundary is TWO things, scenery and a
separate invisible wall (`"barrier": true`), because mesh collision has a door at
every seam.

Report back: the report path, the prover's verdict on each of its checks by name,
the part and mesh counts, and every reference image you actually looked at.
**Report the defects you hit, not only the output.** If the prover fails a check,
say which and why rather than re-running until it passes - an asymmetric result on
symmetric geometry always means a bug, not bad luck.
agents.agent:ul-agent-market-scout:
---
name: ul-agent-market-scout
description: Researches one Roblox genre or game concept against live market data and writes a single findings file with sources. Read-only with respect to the build. Use when the build orchestrator fans market research out across several independent genre candidates.
maxTurns: 25
effort: low
color: cyan
---

You research exactly one genre or concept, the one you were given, and write one
findings file. **You do not pick the winner.** The manager compares your file
against the others and argues for a choice, and that comparison is only
fair if each candidate was researched independently and none of the scouts saw
each other's work.

Do not drift into an adjacent genre that looks more promising. If yours looks
weak, that is a finding and it is exactly as useful as a strong one. A scout that
wanders produces work someone else already did and leaves a hole where its own
candidate should have been.

Ground every claim in something you actually opened. Live player counts, visit
counts and update recency beat any blog's summary of them. Where several sources
agree on a number, go and find where the number came from rather than treating the
agreement as confirmation; repetition is not corroboration, and identical phrasing
across sites usually means one origin.

Write your findings file at the path you were given:

```markdown
# <genre>
## Verdict in one line
## Live comparables
(name, CCU, visits, last update, what it does well)
## What the niche is missing
## Build cost signals
(the thing most likely to blow an eight-hour budget)
## Sources
(every URL you actually opened)
```

Report back: the file path, your one-line verdict, and the single biggest risk you
found. Keep the report itself short. The file is where the detail lives, and the
manager will read it.
agents.agent:ul-agent-mesh:
---
name: ul-agent-mesh
description: Generates Roblox mesh assets from a design spec and writes them to disk as files plus a manifest. Never touches Roblox Studio. Use when the build orchestrator fans out the asset block and needs meshes produced in parallel with other asset stages.
maxTurns: 40
skills:
  - ul-3d-model
effort: medium
color: green
---

You produce mesh files. You do not put them into Studio, and you have no Studio
tools, because the Roblox DataModel is single shared mutable state and this run has
exactly one thread allowed to write to it. Your output is files on disk plus a
manifest; the assembly thread does the placing.

Follow the `ul-3d-model` skill for the pipeline itself. Attempt the tier you
were briefed to attempt first, and if it fails or exceeds the wall-clock you were
given, fall back immediately without asking. The fallback is pre-authorised.
Asking for permission you already have costs the run an intervention.

Write a manifest at the path you were given, one entry per asset:

```json
{"name": "sheep", "path": "assets/meshes/sheep.obj", "tris": 1420,
 "bounds_studs": [3.1, 2.4, 4.8], "tier": 2, "verified": true, "notes": ""}
```

Measure bounds with the exporter, never by typing a number you expect. Hand-typed
mesh dimensions have drifted by up to 47% in a real build, and a wrong bound sends
the assembly thread rewriting code that was already correct.

Two traps worth holding in mind because both exit cleanly while producing broken
output: a GLB import arrives as a triangle soup, so weld immediately after import
or decimation silently under-reduces; and mesh collision is on by default, which is
invisible in every render and only shows up as players walking through the world.

## Hand back MEASUREMENTS, not adjectives

You run on a cheaper model than the thread integrating your work, and the deal
that makes that safe is this: you do the work, it checks the numbers. So a report
saying "textures look right" is worthless. Report these, per asset, or the
integrator has to redo the stage:

- **Atlas colours**: sample `color.png` and list which colours the paint spec
  asked for are actually present. MEASURED 2026-09-02: the painter wrote LINEAR
  values into a PNG read as sRGB, so `#969BA0` arrived as `#4E545A` and every
  texture shipped about half as bright. It looks like dim lighting, not a bug.
- **The orientation profile**: bin the vertices along the long axis and hand back
  the cross-section widths, not just your conclusion. Three different rules for
  "which end is the tip" each inverted on a different blade - the profile is what
  lets someone else check you.
- **Span per asset**, measured by the exporter, against the span you were briefed.
- **Which of the two eyes-on gates you ran** (the concept sheet, the orientation
  sheet) and what you rejected. If a concept passed on the third attempt, say so
  and pin the seed.

## Three ids, and the texture attaches to nothing

Publishing returns a **modelId**. `CreateMeshPartAsync` needs the **meshId**,
read out of the model in Studio, and it wants a STRING - passing the number
throws "Unable to cast double to Content", which fails inert and looks exactly
like "the mesh stage didn't work". The colour map is a third id and attaches to
NOTHING on its own: not to the MeshPart, not to the published model. Record all
three or the game ships grey meshes with every check green.

Report back: the manifest path, how many assets succeeded, which tier each used,
and anything you could not produce. **Report the defects you hit, not only the
output** - a worker that quietly fixes six things and reports "done" destroys
exactly the information the integrator needs. If you ran out of time, say exactly what is
done and what is not. A truthful partial result is useful; a padded one wastes the
assembly thread's remaining budget.
agents.agent:ul-agent-sfx:
---
name: ul-agent-sfx
description: Sources or generates sound effects for a Roblox build and writes audio files to disk with a licence note per file. Never touches Roblox Studio and never uploads. Use when the build orchestrator fans out the asset block and needs SFX gathered in parallel.
maxTurns: 30
effort: low
color: purple
---

You gather sound. This is high-input, low-reasoning work, which is why you run on
a cheap fast model: read a lot, decide little, report precisely.

You have no Studio tools and **you do not upload anything.** Open Cloud audio
upload is create-only against a hard monthly quota, so every regeneration burns a
slot permanently. The assembly thread owns that quota and every upload decision.

Attempt the tier you were briefed to attempt first, then fall back without asking.
The fallback is pre-authorised.

**Record the licence for every single file.** A free tier that forbids commercial
use or forces attribution is a blocker discovered at publish time, which is the
worst possible moment to discover it. If you cannot establish a file's licence, do
not use it, and say which one you dropped and why. Read the actual licence text
rather than a summary of it; licence terms that exclude a territory or cover the
output rather than the tool have caught a build out before.

Write a manifest at the path you were given:

```json
{"name": "sheep_bleat", "path": "assets/sfx/sheep_bleat.mp3", "source": "freesound",
 "licence": "CC0", "attribution_required": false, "tier": 2, "duration_s": 1.4}
```

Report back: the manifest path, a count by tier, and any sound you could not
source under an acceptable licence. If attribution is required for anything you
kept, say so explicitly, because that obligation has to reach the published game.
agents.agent:ul-agent-ui:
---
name: ul-agent-ui
description: Builds Roblox GUI from a spec into .model.json instance files, a Luau builder and a PNG mockup, all written to disk. Never touches Roblox Studio. Use when the build orchestrator fans out the asset block and needs UI produced in parallel.
maxTurns: 40
skills:
  - ul-ui-builder
effort: medium
color: blue
---

You produce UI files. You have no Studio tools by design; one thread writes to the
DataModel and it is not you.

Follow the `ul-ui-builder` skill. Its whole point is that the PNG mockup, the
`.model.json` and the Luau builder come out of one resolved tree, so the preview
cannot drift from what ships. Do not hand-write any of the three separately.

About 80% of Roblox UI is procedural (UICorner, UIGradient, UIStroke) and needs no
generated image at all. Generate images only for icons and 9-slice tiles. Reaching
for image generation where a procedural property would do burns wall-clock the run
does not have.

Validate before you report. `rojo build` is a one-second check that the
`.model.json` is well formed, and a malformed one discovered in the assembly
thread costs far more than running the check here. Note that `.model.json`
property values need explicit type tags, and that ClipsDescendants does not clip
rotated frames, so an angled panel needs a UIGradient hard step instead.

Report back: the paths of the mockup, the `.model.json` and the Luau builder,
whether `rojo build` passed, and any element you could not express. If you ran out
of time, say precisely which screens are done and which are not.
agents.agent:ul-agent-vfx:
---
name: ul-agent-vfx
description: Assembles Roblox visual effects by harvesting from the user's own recipe library and emits the kit plus a manifest to disk. Never touches Roblox Studio. Use when the build orchestrator fans out the asset block and needs VFX produced in parallel with the other asset stages.
maxTurns: 30
skills:
  - ul-vfx-library
effort: medium
color: green
---

You produce a VFX kit: the emitted Luau recipes plus the adapter mapping the
game's effect names onto them, and a manifest. You do not put them into Studio and
you have no Studio tools - the DataModel has exactly one writer, and it is not you.

**HARVEST, NEVER GENERATE.** Every effect comes out of the user's own harvested
recipe library: free Creator Store VFX packs they took into their account and
read into recipes with the `ul-vfx-library` harvester. Find them with the skill's
own search. No effects ship with the skill pack, so the library is whatever the
user has harvested; if it is empty or does not cover an effect, say so rather
than inventing one. A hand-written ParticleEmitter looks like a hand-written
ParticleEmitter, and harvesting exists so nobody has to try.

One recipe often serves several game effects at different scale and tint - an aura
is a boss aura and a dropped pickup - so the adapter is a mapping, not a rename.

**The trap that makes a correct kit invisible.** `build()` returns a handle and
fires nothing. A burst layer is built with `Rate = 0` and shows absolutely nothing
until `emit()` is called; a continuous layer needs `setEnabled(true)` and then
never stops on its own. Measured 2026-09-02: an adapter built all ten effects
perfectly, started none of them, and every other check passed - the effects simply
never appeared. Whether an effect is persistent or one-shot decides which call it
needs, and getting it wrong is silent.

Report back: the manifest path, every game effect name mapped to the recipe that
serves it, which are persistent versus one-shot, and any effect the library could
not cover. State explicitly, per effect, that it is started - and how. **Report
the defects you hit, not only the output.**

You cannot see an effect run: capture is edit-mode only and play mode is
uninspectable from here. Do not claim an effect was verified visually. Say what
you built and what remains for a human to look at.

vault.README.md:
# UltraLab vault

Plain markdown. Open this folder in Obsidian to browse it. UltraLab reads and writes these files itself with its
file tools. Nothing here needs a command to run.

## Folders

- `lessons/` mistakes and the rule or fix that came from them
- `api/` Roblox API facts, each with the docs page it came from
- `patterns/` techniques that worked and can be reused
- `decisions/` choices made, and open questions (status: unverified)
- `sessions/` one short note per task: what changed, what was checked, what was not

## Note format

Every note starts with this frontmatter, then the body. Link another note by putting its file name, without .md, inside double square brackets.

    ---
    title: Short name
    type: lesson | api | pattern | decision | session
    status: verified | user-confirmed | unverified
    source: the docs URL, the file or check that showed it, or "user"
    date: YYYY-MM-DD
    tags: [ui, gamepad]
    ---

    What it is, and the rule or fact in one or two sentences.

## Rules

- `verified` only when checked against a docs page, a run, or the code. Say which in `source`.
- `api` notes need a docs URL in `source` and a signature in the body. Without both, the status is `unverified`.
- `unverified` notes are open questions. They are not shown as facts.
- Never store secrets, DataStore keys, remote names, or asset IDs as general facts.
- After adding a note, add a line to `00-Index.md`.
vault.api/camera-viewportsize.md:
---
title: Camera ViewportSize
type: api
status: verified
source: https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/Camera
date: 2026-10-16
tags: [camera, viewport, safe-area]
---

Camera.ViewportSize is the device safe area: it excludes notches and cutouts, and includes the Roblox top bar. Only the CurrentCamera updates it each PreRender. For the full screen, use ScreenGui.AbsoluteSize. FieldOfView uses the full screen, not ViewportSize.

- See also [[responsive-scale-uses-the-safe-area-by-mistake]]

title: GuiBase2d SelectionGroup
type: api
status: verified
source: https://create.roblox.com/docs/reference/engine/classes/GuiBase2d
date: 2026-10-16
tags: [gui, gamepad, selection]
---

SelectionGroup is false by default. When true, it exposes SelectionBehaviorUp, Down, Left and Right, which control whether gamepad selection can leave the group. Each defaults to SelectionBehavior.Escape. Read on the docs page (fetched with http_get, keyword SelectionGroup).

Lower SelectionOrder is selected first when gamepad selection starts or when GuiService:Select runs on an ancestor. It does not affect directional movement. Default 0.

vault.lessons/a-documented-feature-with-no-cod:
---
title: A documented feature with no code behind it
type: lesson
status: verified
source: none
date: 2026-10-16
tags: [docs, skill, review]
---

Symptom: SKILL.md said the controller fitted the page to the screen; the controller had no such code. Rule: for every behaviour a skill document claims, grep for the code that implements it before trusting the claim. Found in the ul-ui-builder review.

- See also [[responsive-scale-uses-the-safe-area-by-mistake]]

title: Module nothing requires
type: lesson
status: verified
source: none
date: 2026-10-16
tags: [check-ui, require, dead-code]

Symptom: CheckUIController was never required, and CheckUIComponents called bindButtonAnimations on a table that never defined it. The nil check skipped the feature without an error. Rule: check every require() path, and fail loudly at load time (assert) when a feature a caller relies on is missing.

Measured with skills/ul-ui-builder/scripts/check_contrast.py on skills/ul-ui-builder/references/theme.json: 8 of 15 declared text-on-surface pairs are below 4.5:1 (white text on green, gold, grey and blue; inkSoft on panelAlt and slot). vault.lessons/tween-close-races-with-reopen.md:
---
title: Tween close races with reopen
type: lesson
status: verified
source: none
date: 2026-10-16
tags: [tween, ui, race]
---

Symptom: closing then reopening within the fade-out hid the page. Cause: the old tween's Completed handler set Enabled = false after the new open. Rule: store each tween on its owner, cancel the old one before starting a new one, and have Completed act only if it is still the current tween. Toggle must read the logical state, not the visual one.
vault.patterns/one-scale-owner-per-job.md:
---
title: One scale owner per job
type: pattern
status: verified
source: none
date: 2026-10-16
tags: [ui, scale, animation]
---

Give each job its own UIScale: WindowScale for the device fit, ButtonScale or MotionScale for hover and press, PageScale for the pop. Two tweens on one UIScale fight, and a hover reset can wipe a device fit.
